Leaf nodes (inputs): variables or constants. Interior nodes (operations): +, ×, exp, σ, etc. Edges: data flow — the output of one node feeds into the next. Every modern deep-learning framework (PyTorch, JAX, TensorFlow) builds a computation graph behind the scenes. 4 / 64 Simplest Possible Example: f = a + b a b + f Two inputs flow into an addition node; the output is f . That’s it — computation graphs can be very simple. 5 / 64 A Slightly Bigger Example: f = (a + b) × c We decompose into elementary operations: f =d ×c d = a + b, a b c + d × f 6 / 64 Why Decompose into Elementary Operations? 1 Each elementary operation has a known, simple derivative. 2 We can compute the derivative of the whole expression by chaining these simple derivatives together. 3 This is backpropagation — the chain rule applied systematically on a graph. Think of it as “divide and conquer” for differentiation. 7 / 64 Part II The Forward Pass 8 / 64 Forward Pass = Evaluate the Expression Given concrete input values, we propagate them forward through the graph, computing each node’s output. Example: f = (a + b) × c with a = 2, b = 1, c = 4. a=2 b=1 c=4 + d =? × f =? 9 / 64 Forward Pass: Step by Step Step 1: Compute d = a + b = 2 + 1 = 3. a=2 b=1 c=4 + d =3 × f =? 10 / 64 Forward Pass: Step by Step Step 1: Compute d = a + b = 2 + 1 = 3. a=2 b=1 c=4 + d =3 × f =? Step 2: Compute f = d × c = 3 × 4 = 12. 10 / 64 Part III Local Derivatives 11 / 64 What is a Local Derivative? At each operation node, we can compute the derivative of its output with respect to each of its inputs. These are called local derivatives (or local gradients). Addition node: d = a + b ∂d = 1, ∂a ∂d =1 ∂b ∂f = c, ∂d ∂f =d ∂c Multiplication node: f = d × c Addition distributes gradients equally; multiplication “swaps” its inputs. 12 / 64 Annotating the Graph with Local Derivatives a=2 c=4 b=1 ∂d =1 ∂a ∂d =1 ∂b ∂f =d =3 ∂c + ∂f =c=4 ∂d d =3 × f = 12 Each edge now carries a local derivative (blue), the “building blocks” for backward pass. 13 / 64 Part IV The Backward Pass (Backpropagation) 14 / 64 The Goal of the Backward Pass We want to compute: ∂f ∂f ∂f , , ∂a ∂b ∂c i.e. how the final output f changes when each input is perturbed. Strategy: Start at the output, work backwards, applying the chain rule at each node. 15 / 64 Backward Pass: Initialize Seed: The derivative of f with respect to itself is 1. ∂f =1 ∂f This is always our starting point. Think of it as: “if f changes by ϵ, then f changes by ϵ.” Trivially true. 16 / 64 Backward Pass: Step 1 — Through the Multiply Node The × node computes f = d × c. By the chain rule: ∂f ∂f ∂f = × =1×c =1×4=4 ∂d ∂f ∂d ∂f ∂f ∂f = × =1×d =1×3=3 ∂c ∂f ∂c 17 / 64 Backward Pass: Step 1 — Through the Multiply Node The × node computes f = d × c. title: Pop-up Quiz and Answers
sub: Distributional semantics
section: Part II · Distributional Semantics and Neural Networks
text: Pop-Up Quiz: Distributional Semantics & Word2Vec CS115 – Spring 2026 James Pustejovsky 1. Distributional Hypothesis: State the distributional hypothesis in your own words and explain why it provides a foundation for vector space semantics. Answer: The distributional hypothesis states that words occurring in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings (often summarized as “you shall know a word by the company it keeps”). This provides a foundation for vector space semantics because we can represent words as vectors based on their contextual distributions, where similarity in vector space (e.g., cosine similarity) corresponds to semantic similarity. The hypothesis allows us to learn semantic representations from observable co-occurrence patterns in text without manual semantic annotations. 2. CBOW vs Skip-gram: What is the key architectural difference between Continuous Bag of Words (CBOW) and Skip-gram models in word2vec? Which typically performs better for rare words and why? Answer: CBOW predicts a target word from its surrounding context words (many-to-one), while Skip-gram predicts context words from a target word (one-to-many). Skip-gram typically performs better for rare words because each occurrence of a rare word generates multiple training examples (one for each context word), providing more learning signal. CBOW, by contrast, treats each target word occurrence as a single training example regardless of context size. 3. Training Objective: Write the Skip-gram objective function for word2vec. What is being maximized during training? Answer: The Skip-gram objective maximizes the average log probability of context words given target words: T 1X X log p(wt+j | wt ) J(θ) = T t=1 −c≤j≤c,j̸=0 where T is the corpus size, c is the context window size, and wt is the target word. The probability is typically computed using softmax: exp(vw′ O ⊤ vwI ) p(wO | wI ) = PW ′ ⊤ w=1 exp(vw vwI ) 1 Training maximizes the likelihood that words appearing together in contexts have high dot product similarity in the embedding space. 4. Negative Sampling: Explain why negative sampling is used in word2vec training. What computational problem does it solve, and how does it approximate the full softmax? Answer: Negative sampling addresses the computational expense of the softmax normalization term, which requires summing over the entire vocabulary (often 100K+ words) for each training example. Instead of computing the full softmax, negative sampling reformulates the problem as binary classification: distinguishing observed word pairs (positive examples) from randomly sampled noise pairs (negative examples). For each positive pair (wt , wc ), we sample k negative context words from a noise distribution and maximize: log σ(vw′ c ⊤ vwt ) + k X Ewi ∼Pn (w) [log σ(−vw′ i ⊤ vwt )] i=1 This reduces complexity from O(|V |) to O(k) per training example, where typically k = 5– 20. 5. Context Windows: How does the choice of context window size affect the semantic properties captured by word2vec embeddings? Contrast small vs. large windows. Answer: Small context windows (2–5 words) tend to capture syntactic and functional similarities, producing embeddings where words are similar if they can substitute for each other in sentences (paradigmatic relations). For example, “Monday” and “Tuesday” become similar. Large context windows (10+ words) capture broader topical and associative relationships (syntagmatic relations), where words that frequently appear in discussions of the same topics become similar. For example, “doctor” and “hospital” might be more associated with larger windows. The window size thus controls the granularity and type of semantic information encoded. 6. Vector Arithmetic: The famous analogy “king - man + woman ≈ queen” suggests that word2vec captures certain semantic relationships. What linear algebraic property of the embedding space makes such analogies possible? Answer: Word2vec embeddings exhibit linear substructure where semantic relationships correspond to consistent vector offsets. The difference vector vking − vman captures a “royalty” or “male-to-royal” transformation that is approximately parallel to vqueen − vwoman . This property emerges because the Skip-gram objective with negative sampling implicitly factorizes a shifted PMI matrix, and similar relational patterns in the data create similar vector geometry. The embedding space thus develops a coordinate system where certain dimensions correspond to semantic features, allowing algebraic operations to compose and manipulate these features. 2 7. PMI Connection: Explain the relationship between word2vec’s Skip-gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) and Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI). What matrix is word2vec implicitly factorizing? Answer: Levy and Goldberg (2014) showed that SGNS implicitly performs dimensionality reduction on a shifted PMI matrix. Specifically, the optimal Skip-gram solution with negative sampling minimizes a loss function that is equivalent to factorizing a matrix M where: Mij = PMI(wi , wj ) − log k where k is the number of negative samples. The word and context embeddings are lowrank factors that approximately reconstruct this shifted PMI matrix. This connection provides theoretical insight: word2vec learns to represent which word pairs co-occur more than expected by chance (positive PMI) while the shift accounts for the sampling of negative examples. 8. Subsampling: Word2vec uses subsampling to randomly remove frequent words during training. Why is this beneficial for learning high-quality embeddings? Answer: Subsampling addresses the imbalance between frequent and infrequent words. Very frequent words (like “the”, “is”, “of”) appear in many contexts but often carry little semantic content, and their overwhelming presence can dominate training and obscure more meaningful patterns. By probabilistically discarding frequent words (with probability proportional to their frequency), subsampling: (1) speeds up training, (2) balances the representation of rare vs. common words, and (3) allows the model to better capture semantic relationships among content words rather than justpsyntactic function patterns. The subsampling probability is typically P (discard w) = 1− t/f (w) where f (w) is word frequency and t is a threshold (commonly 10−5 ). 9. Out-of-Vocabulary: What is a fundamental limitation of word2vec regarding out-ofvocabulary (OOV) words? How do subword-based approaches like fastText address this issue? Answer: Word2vec maintains a fixed vocabulary learned during training and cannot generate embeddings for OOV words—words not seen during training or misspellings. This is because each word is treated as an atomic unit with its own embedding vector. FastText addresses this by representing words as bags of character n-grams (e.g., “where” becomes ⟨wh, whe, her, ere, re⟩ plus ⟨where⟩). The word embedding is the sum of its n-gram embeddings. For OOV words, fastText can compose an embedding from known character n-grams, enabling generalization to new words and robustness to spelling variations. This is particularly valuable for morphologically rich languages. 10. Evaluation: Name two common intrinsic evaluation methods for word embeddings and one extrinsic evaluation approach. What are the limitations of relying solely on intrinsic evaluations? 3 Answer: Common intrinsic evaluations include: (1) Word similarity tasks where embedding cosine similarities are correlated with human similarity judgments (e.g., WordSim353, SimLex-999), and (2) Analogy tasks where the model solves proportional analogies like “king:man::queen:?” using vector arithmetic. An extrinsic evaluation embeds word2vec vectors into downstream tasks like text classification, named entity recognition, or sentiment analysis and measures task performance. The limitation of intrinsic evaluations is that high performance doesn’t guarantee utility for actual applications. Different tasks may require different semantic properties, and word similarity datasets are often small, domain-specific, and may not reflect the semantic distinctions needed for particular applications. Extrinsic evaluation on target tasks provides more reliable evidence of embedding quality for intended use cases. 4

James Pustejovsky Structured Prediction for Sequences February 13, 2026 17 / 48 From Binary to Structured Perceptron Binary Perceptron (Rosenblatt 1958): Linear classifier: y = sign(w⊤ x) Update rule: If y ̸= ŷ , then w ← w + y x Structured Perceptron (Collins 2002): Score entire structures: score(x, y) = w⊤ Φ(x, y) Prediction: ŷ = arg maxy′ w⊤ Φ(x, y′ ) Update: If y ̸= ŷ, then w ← w + Φ(x, y) − Φ(x, ŷ) Intuition: Increase score of correct structure, decrease score of predicted structure James Pustejovsky Structured Prediction for Sequences February 13, 2026 18 / 48 Structured Perceptron: Formal Algorithm Algorithm 1 Structured Perceptron 1: Initialize w = 0 2: for t = 1 to T (epochs) do 3: for each (x, y) in training data do 4: Predict: ŷ = arg maxy′ ∈Y n w⊤ Φ(x, y′ ) 5: if ŷ ̸= y then 6: Update: w ← w + Φ(x, y) − Φ(x, ŷ) 7: end if 8: end for 9: end for 10: return w Key components: 1 Feature function Φ(x, y) 2 Inference algorithm (Viterbi for sequences) 3 Simple online learning (no probabilistic training) James Pustejovsky Structured Prediction for Sequences // Viterbi February 13, 2026 19 / 48 Why Does Structured Perceptron Work? Theorem (Collins 2002): If data is separable with margin γ, structured perceptron makes at most R 2 /γ 2 mistakes, where R = maxx,y ||Φ(x, y)|| Intuition: Perceptron moves towards correct structure Increases dot product w⊤ Φ(x, y) for gold structures Decreases dot product for incorrect predictions Eventually separates correct from incorrect (if separable) Advantages: Simple to implement No need for partition function (unlike CRF) Fast training Often competitive accuracy James Pustejovsky Structured Prediction for Sequences February 13, 2026 20 / 48 Averaged Perceptron Problem: Final weights Solution: Monitor performance on validation set 1 2 Split data: train / dev / test After each epoch: Run Viterbi on dev set Compute accuracy 3 Keep weights from epoch with best dev accuracy 4 Report entities James Pustejovsky Structured Prediction for Sequences February 13, 2026 28 / 48 Inference: Constraint Incorporation Viterbi finds: arg maxy w⊤ Φ(x, y) Can easily incorporate hard constraints: Example (NER): ”I-PER must follow B-PER or I-PER” During Viterbi, set s(y ′ , y ) = −∞ for invalid transitions Ensures output respects BIO constraints Example (POS): ”DET cannot follow DET” Encode linguistic constraints into transition scores Advantage over neural softmax: Guaranteed valid outputs James Pustejovsky Structured Prediction for Sequences February 13, 2026 29 / 48 Beam Search: Approximate Inference Problem: For some tasks, exact inference is intractable Beam search: Keep top-k hypotheses at each step 1 2 Initialize: beam = {(ϵ, 0)} (empty sequence, score 0) For position i = 1 to n: For each hypothesis (y1:i−1 , s) in beam: Expand with all possible tags yi ∈ Y Compute scores for all expansions Keep top-k by total score 3 Return best complete hypothesis Complexity: O(nkK ) most problematic incorrect prediction (violates margin most) Connection to structured SVM: Max-margin training James Pustejovsky Structured Prediction for Sequences February 13, 2026 31 / 48 y(i) Interpretation: Gold structure should score higher than any other by at least the loss Training: Cutting plane algorithm (iterate: find most violated constraint, add to working set) Advantage over perceptron: Regularization, margin-based James Pustejovsky Structured Prediction for Sequences February 13, 2026 32 / 48 Higher-Order Models So far: First-order (bigram) transitions score(x, y) = n X s(yi−1 , yi , x, i) i=1 Higher-order: Trigram, skip-chain, etc. score(x, y) = n X s(yi−2 , yi−1 , yi , x, i) i=1 Trade-offs: More expressive (capture longer dependencies) Slower inference: O(nK 3 ) for trigrams Sparser features (data fragmentation) Practical: Second-order often good balance James Pustejovsky Structured Prediction for Sequences February 13, 2026 33 / 48 Semi-Markov Models Standard sequence labeling: One label per token Semi-Markov CRF: Segment-based labeling Output: sequence of segments with labels Example (NER): [Steve Jobs]PER [founded]O [Apple]ORG Advantages: Features on entire segments (not just tokens) Natural for chunking tasks Can capture segment-level properties Inference: Dynamic programming over segments (O(nL2 K 2 ) where L is max segment length) James Pustejovsky Structured Prediction for Sequences February 13, 2026 34 / 48 From Linear to Neural Models Linear structured models: score(x, y) = w⊤ Φ(x, y) Features Φ are hand-crafted, sparse, discrete Neural structured models: score(x, y) = n X w⊤ fθ (xi , xi−1 , . . .) + s(yi−1 , yi ) i=1 where fθ is a neural network (LSTM, Transformer) Neural+CRF (BiLSTM-CRF): BiLSTM computes contextual representations CRF layer models transitions Train end-to-end with backprop This bridges to your next lectures on RNNs and attention! CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 18 / 59 Viterbi: Position 2 (continued) For tag VERB at position 2: From DET: 5.0 + (−0.5) + 0.0 = 4.5 From NOUN: 0.5 + 0.0 + 0.0 = 0.5 δ2 (VERB) = 4.5, ψ2 (VERB) = DET After position 2: Tag δ2 ψ2 NOUN VERB DET 9.0 4.5 3.5 DET DET DET Best path to ”dog” as NOUN: START → DET → NOUN (score 9.0) CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 19 / 59 Viterbi: Position 3 (”runs”) For tag VERB at position 3: From NOUN: 9.0 + 1.8 + 2.0 = 12.8 From VERB: 4.5 + 0.5 + 2.0 = 7.0 From DET: 3.5 + (−1.0) + 2.0 = 4.5 δ3 (VERB) = 12.8, ψ3 (VERB) = NOUN Best final tag: VERB with score 12.8 Backtrack: Position 3: VERB (best ending) Position 2: ψ3 (VERB) = NOUN Position 1: ψ2 (NOUN) = DET Final prediction: DET NOUN VERB CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 20 / 59 Viterbi: Complexity Analysis Time complexity: O(nK 2 ) n positions in sequence K possible tags For each position and tag, consider K previous tags Space complexity: O(nK ) Store δ and ψ tables Example: Sentence length: n = 20 words Penn Treebank: K = 45 tags Operations: 20 × 452 = 40, 500 (very fast!) Compare to naive enumeration: 4520 ≈ 1033 sequences! CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 21 / 59 Handling Unknown Words Problem: Test data contains words not seen in training Solution 1: Morphological features Prefixes/suffixes: ”ing” suggests VERB, ”tion” suggests NOUN Capitalization: mid-sentence capitals often PROPN Contains-digit: often NUM Contains-hyphen: often ADJ Solution 2: Word shape ”Xxxx” (capitalized) → likely PROPN ”xxxx” (lowercase) → various ”XXXX” (all caps) → acronym, PROPN ”dd/dd/dddd” → DATE Key insight: These features generalize beyond the training vocabulary! CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 22 / 59 Example: Unknown Word Features Unknown word: ”unbelievable” Even if never seen in training, features capture: ⟨yi , prefix=un⟩ (negative prefix) ⟨yi , suffix=able⟩ (adjective suffix) ⟨yi , suffix=ble⟩ ⟨yi , suffix=le⟩ ⟨yi , len > 10⟩ If training data had: ”comfortable” / ADJ ”reasonable” / ADJ ”unbelievable” gets tagged as ADJ via suffix pattern! This is why feature engineering matters! CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 23 / 59 Feature Engineering Best Practices Good features are: 1 Informative: Correlate with correct tags 2 Generalizable: Work beyond training examples 3 Sparse: Most features = 0 for any input Common patterns: Start simple (word + tag, bigram transitions) Add context (previous/next words) Add morphology (affixes, shape) Add conjunctions (word + previous tag) Test and iterate! Overfitting risk: Too many rare features → memorize training data Solution: Feature count cutoffs (e.g., appears ≥ 5 times) CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 24 / 59 Named Entity Recognition (NER) Task: Identify and classify named entities in text Example: Barack B-PER Obama I-PER visited O Microsoft B-ORG in O Seattle B-LOC . O Entity types: PER (person), ORG (organization), LOC (location), MISC (miscellaneous) BIO tagging scheme: B-X: Beginning of entity type X I-X: Inside entity type X (continuation) O: Outside any entity With 4 entity types: 4 × 2 + 1 = 9 tags total CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 25 / 59 Why BIO Tagging? Question: Why not just use entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, O)? Problem: Adjacent entities of same type United ORG Airlines ORG beat O American ORG Without B/I distinction: Can’t tell if ”United Airlines” is one entity or two! With BIO: United B-ORG Airlines I-ORG beat O American B-ORG Clear: ”United Airlines” is one ORG, ”American” is another B- tag marks entity boundaries CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 26 / 59 BIO Constraints Valid transitions: O → O, O → B-X (for any X) B-X → I-X, B-X → O, B-X → B-Y (for any Y) I-X → I-X, I-X → O, I-X → B-Y (for any Y) Invalid transitions: O → I-X (can’t continue entity without starting it!) I-PER → I-ORG (can’t change entity type mid-entity) Enforcement: During Viterbi: Set score to −∞ for invalid transitions Guarantees structurally valid output This is a key advantage of structured prediction! CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 27 / 59 Running Example for NER Training sentence: Tim B-PER Cook I-PER runs O Apple B-ORG in O California B-LOC . O Entity mentions: Person: ”Tim Cook” Organization: ”Apple” Location: ”California” We’ll explore: 1 Features specific to NER 2 How capitalization and context matter 3 Multi-word entity handling 4 Training dynamics CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 28 / 59 Feature Templates for NER Word-level features: ⟨yi , xi ⟩, ⟨yi , lowercase(xi )⟩ ⟨yi , is-capitalized(xi )⟩ (crucial for NER!) ⟨yi , is-all-caps(xi )⟩ ⟨yi , word-shape(xi )⟩ (e.g., ”Xxxx”, ”XX”) Affix features: ⟨yi , suffix(xi , k)⟩ for k = 1, 2, 3 Helpful for organizations: ”-Corp”, ”-Inc”, ”-Ltd” Context features: ⟨yi , xi−1 , xi+1 ⟩ (both neighbors) ⟨yi , xi−2 , xi−1 ⟩ (left bigram context) Gazetteers (optional): ⟨yi , in-person-list(xi )⟩ ⟨yi , in-location-list(xi )⟩ CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 29 / 59 Features for ”Tim Cook runs Apple...” Position 1: ”Tim” / B-PER ⟨START, B-PER⟩ (transition) ⟨B-PER, Tim⟩ (emission) ⟨B-PER, tim⟩ (lowercase) ⟨B-PER, capitalized=True⟩ ← Key! ⟨B-PER, shape=Xxx⟩ ⟨B-PER, next=Cook⟩ (right context) ⟨B-PER, im⟩ (suffix) Why capitalization matters: Mid-sentence capital → likely entity ”tim” (lowercase) would rarely be B-PER CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 30 / 59 Features for ”Tim Cook runs Apple...” (cont.) Position 2: ”Cook” / I-PER ⟨B-PER, I-PER⟩ (transition from B-PER) ⟨I-PER, Cook⟩ (emission) ⟨I-PER, capitalized=True⟩ ⟨I-PER, prev=Tim⟩ (left context) Position 3: ”runs” / O ⟨I-PER, O⟩ (transition ending entity) ⟨O, runs⟩ (emission) ⟨O, lowercase=runs⟩ ⟨O, capitalized=False⟩ ← Key! Lowercase mid-sentence word → likely not an entity CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 31 / 59 Features for Multi-word Entity Position 4: ”Apple” / B-ORG ⟨O, B-ORG⟩ (transition) ⟨B-ORG, Apple⟩ (emission) ⟨B-ORG, capitalized=True⟩ ⟨B-ORG, prev=runs⟩ Ambiguity: ”Apple” could be: ORG (the company) ← correct in this context O (the fruit) Context helps: ”runs Apple” suggests company (you can’t ”run” a fruit) Capitalized → more likely entity Features like ⟨B-ORG, prev=runs⟩ learn this! CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 32 / 59 Initial Training: Zero Weights First training example: Tim/B-PER Cook/I-PER runs/O Apple/B-ORG in/O California/B-LOC ./O Initial model: w = 0 Prediction with zero weights: All sequences score 0 Viterbi might predict (tie-breaking): Tim/O Cook/O runs/O Apple/O in/O California/O ./O (Predicts everything as O — common with random initialization!) Update: Increase weights for all gold features Decrease weights for predicted features (mostly O transitions/emissions) CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 33 / 59 After First Update: Key Weights Increased weights (sampled): w [⟨START, B-PER⟩] = +1 w [⟨B-PER, capitalized=True⟩] = +1 w [⟨B-PER, I-PER⟩] = +1 w [⟨I-PER, O⟩] = +1 w [⟨O, B-ORG⟩] = +1 w [⟨B-ORG, Apple⟩] = +1 w [⟨O, B-LOC⟩] = +1 Decreased weights: w [⟨START, O⟩] = −1 w [⟨O, Tim⟩] = −1 w [⟨O, Apple⟩] = −1 Model now prefers: Capitalized words at sentence start → B-PER CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 34 / 59 Second Training Example Example 2: Microsoft/B-ORG hired/O engineers/O in/O Seattle/B-LOC ./O Current model has learned: Sentence-initial capitalized word → likely B-PER (+1) But ”Microsoft” should be B-ORG! Possible prediction: Microsoft/B-PER hired/O engineers/O in/O Seattle/B-LOC ./O (Gets ”Microsoft” wrong) Update effect: w [⟨START, B-ORG⟩] ← +1 w [⟨START, B-PER⟩] ← 0 (was +1, now 0) w [⟨B-ORG, Microsoft⟩] ← +1 Model learns: Some sentence-initial words are ORG, not PER! CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 35 / 59 Learning Entity Boundaries Challenge: Multi-word entities Example 3: New/B-ORG York/I-ORG Times/I-ORG reported/O ... What model learns: w [⟨B-ORG, I-ORG⟩] becomes positive w [⟨I-ORG, I-ORG⟩] becomes positive w [⟨I-ORG, capitalized=True⟩] positive Effect: Consecutive capitalized words → likely single entity B-ORG followed by capitalized word → likely I-ORG I-ORG followed by lowercase → likely end of entity (transition to O) CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 36 / 59 Handling Ambiguity: ”Apple” Challenge: Same word, different labels in different contexts Training examples: 1 ”... runs Apple/B-ORG in ...” 2 ”... ate an apple/O ...” How does model distinguish? Features capture context: ⟨B-ORG, Apple, prev=runs⟩ → positive weight ⟨O, apple, prev=an⟩ → positive weight ⟨B-ORG, capitalized=True⟩ → positive ⟨O, capitalized=False⟩ → positive Capitalization + context words disambiguate! CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 37 / 59 Viterbi with BIO Constraints Sentence: ”Steve Jobs founded Apple” Gold: B-PER I-PER O B-ORG During Viterbi: At position 2 (”Jobs”), consider transitions: From B-PER to I-PER: ✓Valid, compute score From B-PER to I-ORG: ✗ Invalid! Set score = −∞ From O to I-PER: ✗ Invalid! Set score = −∞ Result: Viterbi automatically enforces BIO constraints Never produces invalid sequences No post-processing needed! CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 38 / 59 Detailed Viterbi for NER Sentence: ”Cook founded Apple” Simplified weights: Feature Weight ⟨START, B-PER⟩ ⟨START, O⟩ ⟨B-PER, O⟩ ⟨O, O⟩ ⟨O, Apple⟩ 1.5 0.5 1.2 0.8 -0.5 Feature ⟨B-PER, Cook⟩ ⟨O, Cook⟩ ⟨O, founded⟩ ⟨O, B-ORG⟩ ⟨B-ORG, Apple⟩ Weight 2.0 0.3 1.0 1.5 2.5 Position 1 (”Cook”): δ1 (B-PER) = 1.5 + 2.0 = 3.5 δ1 (O) = 0.5 + 0.3 = 0.8 CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 39 / 59 Detailed Viterbi (continued) Position 2 (”founded”): For tag O: From B-PER: 3.5 + 1.2 + 1.0 = 5.7 From O: 0.8 + 0.8 + 1.0 = 2.6 δ2 (O) = 5.7, ψ2 (O) = B-PER Position 3 (”Apple”): For tag B-ORG: From O: 5.7 + 1.5 + 2.5 = 9.7 From B-PER: invalid transition from pos 2 CS 115B – Spring 2026 δ (B-ORG) = 9.7 3 Perceptron for Sequence Labeling Structured James Pustejovsky 40 / 59 Common NER Errors Error type 1: Boundary errors Gold: ”New/B-LOC York/I-LOC” Pred: ”New/O York/B-LOC” Wrong boundary, right type Error type 2: Type errors Gold: ”Apple/B-ORG” Pred: ”Apple/B-LOC” Right boundaries, wrong type Error type 3: Missed entities Gold: ”Paris/B-LOC” Pred: ”Paris/O” Common with rare entities Evaluation: Exact match (boundaries + type must match) Precision: % of predicted entities that are correct CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 41 / 59 Improving NER Performance Better features: Word embeddings (pre-trained) Character n-grams Brown clusters Gazetteers (lists of known entities) More training data: Manually annotate more examples Use distant supervision (weak labels from KB) Data augmentation Model improvements: Averaged perceptron (vs. standard) Higher-order features (trigrams) Semi-Markov models (segment-level features) CS 115B – Spring 2026 Structured Perceptron for Sequence Labeling James Pustejovsky 42 / 59 Averaged Perceptron Revisit

title: Neural Dependency Parsing
section: Part II · Distributional Semantics and Neural Networks
text: Neural Dependency Parsing CS 115B – Spring 2026 James Pustejovsky February 26, 2026 James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 1 / 59 Roadmap for Today Part I: Dependency Parsing Theory (20 minutes) What are dependencies? Dependency grammar vs. phrase structure Dependency trees and properties Part II: Transition-Based Parsing (25 minutes) Arc-standard transition system Stack, buffer, and actions Complete parsing examples Part III: Chen & Manning Neural Parser (35 minutes) Motivation: Feature engineering problem Neural network architecture Training and inference Detailed examples Part IV: Results and Impact (10 minutes) James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 2 / 59 What is Syntactic Structure? Goal: Represent grammatical relationships between words Two main formalisms: 1. Phrase structure (constituency): Groups words into nested constituents Example: (S (NP The cat) (VP (V sat) (PP (P on) (NP the mat)))) Focus on hierarchical groupings 2. Dependency structure: Direct binary relations between words Example: ”sat” depends on ROOT, ”cat” depends on ”sat” Focus on head-dependent relations Today: Dependency parsing! James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 3 / 59 Dependency Structure: Example Sentence: ”I prefer the morning flight through Denver” root obj det amod nsubj ROOT I prefer the morning nmod flight through pobj Denver Dependencies: ”prefer” is the head of ”I” (subject relation) ”prefer” is the head of ”flight” (object relation) ”flight” is the head of ”the”, ”morning” (modifiers) ”through” is the head of ”Denver” (prepositional object) James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 4 / 59 Dependency Relations Each arc has a label indicating the grammatical relation: Common Universal Dependencies relations: nsubj: Nominal subject (”I” ← ”prefer”) obj: Direct object (”flight” ← ”prefer”) det: Determiner (”the” ← ”flight”) amod: Adjectival modifier (”morning” ← ”flight”) nmod: Nominal modifier (”through” ← ”flight”) case: Case marker (”Denver” ← ”through”) root: Relation to ROOT Universal Dependencies (UD) v2 has 40 core relation types Note: Chen & Manning focus on unlabeled parsing first, then add labels James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 5 / 59 Why Dependencies? Advantages over constituency parsing: 1. Word-to-word relations: Direct connection between ”prefer” and ”flight” No need for intermediate nodes (VP, NP, etc.) Easier for downstream tasks (relation extraction, QA) 2. Better for free word order languages: Czech, Russian, Latin: word order flexible Dependencies capture relations regardless of order 3. Useful for NLP applications: Information extraction: who did what to whom? Machine translation: align dependencies across languages Question answering: find semantic roles James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 6 / 59 Dependency Tree Properties Valid dependency tree must satisfy: 1. Single head: Each word has exactly one head (except ROOT) 2. Acyclic: No cycles (cannot have a → b → c → a) 3. Connected: All words connected to tree 4. Rooted: One unique root node These properties define a spanning tree over the words Projectivity (optional constraint): Tree is projective if no crossing arcs Equivalent to: can draw all arcs above words without crossing Most English sentences are projective Some languages (Czech, Dutch) have more non-projective trees James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 7 / 59 Projective vs. Non-Projective Projective (common in English): obj nsubj I saw a pobj nmod det cat with binoculars No crossing arcs Non-projective (rare in English, common in Czech): nmod:tmod nmod nsubjpass A hearing pobj det auxpass det is scheduled on the issue today ”hearing” linked to ”on” crosses over with ”scheduled” linked to ”today” (non-projective arc) James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 8 / 59 Dependency Parsing Approaches Three main algorithmic families: 1. Graph-based (Eisner, MST): Score all possible arcs Find maximum spanning tree Global optimization, can be non-projective O(n3 ) for projective, O(n2 ) for approximate non-projective 2. Transition-based (shift-reduce): Process words left-to-right Build tree incrementally with actions Greedy or beam search, linear time ← Chen & Manning use this! 3. Hybrid / Neural graph-based: Modern: Dozat & Manning (2017) biaffine parser Encode with BERT, score all arcs with neural network James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 9 / 59 Transition-Based Parsing: Overview Key idea: Build parse tree through sequence of actions Configuration: Stack σ: Partially processed words Buffer β: Remaining words to process Arcs A: Dependencies built so far Actions (arc-standard system): SHIFT: Move first word from buffer to stack LEFT-ARC: Add arc from stack top to second-to-top, remove second-to-top RIGHT-ARC: Add arc from second-to-top to stack top, remove top Goal: Start with all words in buffer, end with all arcs created James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 10 / 59 Arc-Standard Actions: Details Initial configuration: Stack: [ROOT] Buffer: [word1 , word2 , ..., wordn ] Arcs: ∅ Action definitions: SHIFT: (σ, wi |β, A) ⇒ (σ|wi , β, A) Move word from buffer to stack r LEFT-ARCr : (σ|wi |wj , β, A) ⇒ (σ|wj , β, A ∪ {wj − → wi }) Add arc wj (stack top) → wi (second) with label r Remove wi from stack r RIGHT-ARCr : (σ|wi |wj , β, A) ⇒ (σ|wi , β, A ∪ {wi − → wj }) Add arc wi (second) → wj (top) with label r Remove wj from stack James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 11 / 59 Transition Example: ”I eat fish” Sentence: ”I eat fish” Target dependencies: ROOT → eat (root) eat → I (nsubj) eat → fish (obj) Initial state: Stack: [ROOT] Buffer: [I, eat, fish] Arcs: ∅ We’ll trace through the parsing actions step by step... James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 12 / 59 Step 1: SHIFT Action: SHIFT Before: Stack: [ROOT] Buffer: [I, eat, fish] Arcs: ∅ After: Stack: [ROOT, I] Buffer: [eat, fish] Arcs: ∅ Move ”I” from buffer to stack to process it James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 13 / 59 Step 2: SHIFT Action: SHIFT Before: Stack: [ROOT, I] Buffer: [eat, fish] Arcs: ∅ After: Stack: [ROOT, I, eat] Buffer: [fish] Arcs: ∅ Move ”eat” to stack. Now we have ”I” and ”eat” on stack, can create arc James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 14 / 59 Step 3: LEFT-ARC (nsubj) Action: LEFT-ARCnsubj Before: Stack: [ROOT, I, eat] Buffer: [fish] Arcs: ∅ After: Stack: [ROOT, eat] Buffer: [fish] nsubj Arcs: {eat −−−→ I} Create dependency: ”eat” (top) is the head of ”I” (second). Remove ”I” from stack since it’s complete. Notation: Stack top, Second from top James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 15 / 59 Step 4: SHIFT Action: SHIFT Before: Stack: [ROOT, eat] Buffer: [fish] nsubj Arcs: {eat −−−→ I} After: Stack: [ROOT, eat, fish] Buffer: [ ] nsubj Arcs: {eat −−−→ I} Move ”fish” to stack James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 16 / 59 Step 5: RIGHT-ARC (obj) Action: RIGHT-ARCobj Before: Stack: [ROOT, eat, fish] Buffer: [ ] nsubj Arcs: {eat −−−→ I} After: Stack: [ROOT, eat] Buffer: [ ] nsubj obj Arcs: {eat −−−→ I, eat −−→ fish} Create dependency: ”eat” (second) is head of ”fish” (top). Remove ”fish”. James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 17 / 59 Step 6: RIGHT-ARC (root) Action: RIGHT-ARCroot Before: Stack: [ROOT, eat] Buffer: [ ] nsubj obj Arcs: {eat −−−→ I, eat −−→ fish} After: Stack: [ROOT] Buffer: [ ] nsubj obj root Arcs: {eat −−−→ I, eat −−→ fish, ROOT −−→ eat} Parsing complete! Stack has only ROOT, buffer empty, all arcs created. James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 18 / 59 Complete Action Sequence Sentence: ”I eat fish” Step 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 James Pustejovsky Action Stack Buffer — SHIFT SHIFT LEFT-ARCnsubj SHIFT RIGHT-ARCobj RIGHT-ARCroot [ROOT] [ROOT, I] [ROOT, I, eat] [ROOT, eat] [ROOT, eat, fish] [ROOT, eat] [ROOT] [I, eat, fish] [eat, fish] [fish] [fish] [] [] [] Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 19 / 59 Complete Resulting Tree Sentence: ”I eat fish” root obj nsubj ROOT James Pustejovsky I eat Neural Dependency Parsing fish February 26, 2026 20 / 59 Action Preconditions Question: Can we always apply any action? Answer: No! Actions have preconditions: SHIFT: Precondition: Buffer must be non-empty LEFT-ARC: Precondition: Stack must have ≥ 2 elements Additional: Second element cannot be ROOT (ROOT has no head) RIGHT-ARC: Precondition: Stack must have ≥ 2 elements Additional: Top element must not already have a head (single head constraint) Oracle: Supervision signal that tells us the correct action given gold tree James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 21 / 59 Greedy vs. Beam Search Greedy parsing: At each step, pick highest-scoring valid action Fast: O(n) actions for sentence of length n Problem: Early mistakes cannot be corrected Beam search: Maintain top-k partial parses At each step, expand all and keep best k Better accuracy, slower: O(nkA) where A is action count Chen & Manning use greedy (later work adds beam search) Trade-off: Speed vs. accuracy Greedy: 1000 sentences/second Beam search (k=8): 100 sentences/second James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 22 / 59 Traditional Approach: Feature Templates Pre-neural parsers (Nivre, Zhang & Nivre 2011): Feature extraction from configuration: Top 3 words on stack: s1 , s2 , s3 First 3 words in buffer: b1 , b2 , b3 Leftmost/rightmost children of stack words POS tags of these words Dependency labels of existing arcs Example features: Word form: s1 .w , b1 .w , s2 .w POS tag: s1 .t, b1 .t Combinations: ⟨s1 .w , s1 .t⟩, ⟨s1 .w , b1 .w ⟩ Contextual: ⟨s1 .w , s1 .lc.w ⟩ (leftmost child) Typical feature set: 10-20 million sparse binary features! James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 23 / 59 Problems with Feature Templates 1. Incompleteness: Hand-designed features miss important patterns Cannot easily add higher-order features (combinations explode) Expert knowledge required 2. Sparsity: Most features are 0 in any configuration Need millions of training examples to learn weights Rare word combinations never seen 3. Computational cost: Feature extraction is expensive (lookup many templates) 95% of parsing time spent on feature computation! Each configuration: extract features → score actions Chen & Manning’s insight: Use neural network to learn features! James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 24 / 59 Key Innovation: Learned Feature Embeddings Instead of: Millions of sparse binary features Use: Dense continuous embeddings Representation: Words: d-dimensional vectors (e.g., 50-dim) POS tags: d-dimensional vectors Dependency labels: d-dimensional vectors Advantages: Automatic feature learning Generalization: similar words have similar embeddings Dense representation: every word has informative vector Compositional: can combine features easily James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 25 / 59 Input Representation From configuration, extract: Stack elements (Chen & Manning use top 3): s1 , s2 , s3 : Top three words on stack Buffer elements (first 3): b1 , b2 , b3 : First three words in buffer Children (leftmost/rightmost 2 children of s1 , s2 ): lc1 (s1 ), rc1 (s1 ), lc2 (s1 ), rc2 (s1 ) lc1 (s2 ), rc1 (s2 ), lc2 (s2 ), rc2 (s2 ) Total: 18 elements (positions to extract information from) For each element, get: Word embedding POS tag embedding (For children) Dependency label embedding James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 26 / 59 Feature Set Size Token elements: 18 positions For each position: Word: w ∈ Rdw (word embedding) POS tag: t ∈ Rdt (tag embedding) Label: l ∈ Rdl (for children only) Total feature vector: 18 word embeddings: 18 × dw 18 POS tag embeddings: 18 × dt 12 label embeddings (only for children): 12 × dl Example dimensions (Chen & Manning): dw = 50, dt = 50, dl = 50 Total: 18 × 50 + 18 × 50 + 12 × 50 = 2400 dimensions Compare to: 10 million sparse features in traditional parser! James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 27 / 59 Neural Network Architecture SHIFT, LEFT-ARC, RIGHT-ARC, ... Output Layer (Softmax) |A| actions (e.g., 3 unlabeled or 40+ labeled) W2 Hidden Layer ReLU activation 200-dim (configurable) W1 Stack + Buffer + Children James Pustejovsky Input Layer (word + POS + label embeddings) 2400-dim Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 28 / 59 Mathematical Details Input vector x ∈ Rdin : Concatenation of all embeddings: w t t l x = [ew s1 ; es2 ; . . . ; es1 ; es2 ; . . . ; elc1 (s1 ) ; . . .] Hidden layer: h = max(0, W1 x + b1 ) where W1 ∈ Rdh ×din , dh = 200 Output layer (action scores): p = softmax(W2 h + b2 ) where W2 ∈ R|A|×dh Prediction: a∗ = arg maxa pa (among valid actions) James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 29 / 59 Training: Oracle and Loss Training data: Treebank with gold dependency trees Oracle: For each configuration during parsing Determine gold action that leads toward gold tree Dynamic oracle: choose action that keeps gold tree reachable Loss function: Cross-entropy N X log p(ai∗ | ci ) L=− i=1 where ai∗ is gold action for configuration ci Optimization: AdaGrad with mini-batches Learning rate: 0.01 (initial) Dropout on hidden layer (50%) Pre-train word embeddings or random initialization James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 30 / 59 Initialization Strategies Word embeddings: Option 1: Random initialization (Gaussian) Option 2: Pre-trained (word2vec, GloVe) — Better! Fine-tune during training POS tag embeddings: Random initialization (small vocabulary, 45 tags) Learn from scratch Label embeddings: Random initialization ( 40 relations) Learn from scratch Special tokens: NULL: for non-existent children ROOT: special token UNK: unknown words (rare in training) James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 31 / 59 Running Example: ”I eat fish” Let’s trace through the neural parser We’ll see: 1 Configuration at each step 2 Feature extraction (which embeddings) 3 Neural network input 4 Action prediction Assume pre-trained embeddings: 50 (word embedding for ”I”) ew I ∈R etPRON ∈ R50 (POS embedding for pronoun) etc. For clarity, we’ll focus on which embeddings are extracted, not their exact values James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 32 / 59 Initial Configuration Configuration: Stack: [ROOT] Buffer: [I, eat, fish] Arcs: ∅ Feature extraction: Element Word POS s1 s2 s3 b1 b2 b3 lc1 (s1 ), rc1 (s1 ), . . . ROOT NULL NULL I eat fish NULL ROOT NULL NULL PRON VERB NOUN NULL Input vector: Concatenate all embeddings (2400-dim) Network predicts: SHIFT (move ”I” to stack) James Pustejovsky Neural Dependency Parsing February 26, 2026 33 / 59 After First SHIFT Configuration: Stack: [ROOT, I] Buffer: [eat, fish] Arcs: ∅ Feature extraction: Element Word POS s1 s2 s3 b1 b2 b3 I ROOT NULL eat fish NULL PRON ROOT NULL VERB NOUN NULL Network predicts: SHIFT (move ”eat” to stack) Why not LEFT-ARC? title: Introduction to CNNs
section: Part III · Sequence Models: CNNs and RNNs
text: Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP From spatial gradients to semantic n-gram extraction James Pustejovsky March 2026 Graduate Seminar in Computer Science/Computational Linguistics The Geometric Foundation The Failure of the Fully Connected (MLP) Paradigm • High-Dimensional Inputs: A 224 × 224 × 3 image has 150,528 inputs. • Parameter Explosion: A single hidden layer of 1,000 neurons ≈ 150M parameters. • Statistical Inefficiency: MLPs treat pixel (i, j) and (i + 1, j) as independent variables. Inductive Bias: Translation Invariance A feature (e.g., a vertical edge or the word ”not”) has the same identity regardless of its absolute coordinate in space or time. 1 Defining the Discrete 2D Convolution The output at position (i, j) is the element-wise product sum of the input I and kernel K : XX (I ∗ K )i,j = I (i + m, j + n) · K (m, n) m n • Local Connectivity: Neurons only ”see” neighbors within a k × k window. • Weight Sharing: The same weights K are applied across the entire input. 2 Feature Extraction: The Sobel Operator We detect boundaries by calculating the Intensity Gradient:    −1 −2 −1 0 1    Gx = −2 0 2 , Gy =  0 0 1 2 −1 0 1  −1  0 1 • Gx detects horizontal transitions (vertical lines). • Gy detects vertical transitions (horizontal lines). q • |∇G | = Gx2 + Gy2 provides the total edge magnitude. 3 The Mechanics of Sizing: Padding and Stride • Stride (S): The step size of the kernel. S = 2 reduces spatial resolution by half. • Padding (P): Adding zeros to the border. • Valid (P = 0): Output size W − K + 1. Edges are lost. ): Output size matches Input size. • Same (P = K −1 2 The Output Dimension Formula  W − K + 2P Wout = S  +1 4 1D Convolutions in NLP Mapping Space to Time: 1D Sequences In NLP, our ”Image” is a sentence matrix X ∈ Rn×d (Length × Embedding Dim). • Temporal Convolution: The kernel width is fixed to d (full embedding). • Window Size (h): The number of words the kernel ”sees” at once. • Result: A feature map of length n − h + 1. 5 Kernel Size as N-gram Order A 1D kernel acts as a soft n-gram detector: • h = 2: Bigram detector (e.g., ”not happy”). • h = 3: Trigram detector (e.g., ”was not happy”). Unlike traditional n-grams, CNNs use **distributed representations** (embeddings), allowing them to recognize ”not happy” and ”never joyful” with the same filter. 6 Max-Over-Time Pooling How do we handle variable-length sentences for a fixed-size classifier? ĉ = max{c1 , c2 , . . . , cn−h+1 } • Length Invariance: The network finds the ”strongest” feature regardless of where it appears. • Saliency: Discards noise; only the highest activation is passed forward. 7 The Kim (2014) Architecture • Input: Sentence embeddings (Static vs. Non-static). • Multi-Filter Bank: 100 filters for h = 3, 4, 5. • Concatenation: Feature maps are pooled and concatenated into a single vector. • Output: Softmax layer for classification (Sentiment, Intent). 8 Learning and Modern Frontiers How Kernels Learn: Shared-Weight Backpropagation ∂L • The gradient ∂W is calculated for every position where the kernel was applied. • Weight Sharing: Because the same W is used everywhere, the final update is the sum of gradients across all spatial/temporal steps. • This forces the kernel to be a ”Global Detector.” 9 CNNs vs. Transformers in 2026 CNN (Local) Transformer (Global) • Linear complexity O(n). • Quadratic complexity O(n2 ). • High efficiency on edge devices. • Captures long-range dependencies. • Requires massive pre-training. • Better for small datasets. Current SOTA trend: ConvNeXt architectures (CNNs with large 7 × 7 kernels) match Transformers in performance. 10

text: Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP CS 115B – Spring 2026 James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 1/1 Course Context Neural NLP Sequence: 1 Today: CNNs — Local pattern detection 2 Next: RNNs — Sequential processing 3 Then: Attention — Flexible context 4 Finally: LLMs — Large-scale pre-training Why CNNs? Efficient feature extraction Parallelizable (unlike RNNs) Good for local patterns (n-grams) Still used in modern architectures Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 2/1 Roadmap Part I: CNN Basics from Vision (25 min) What is convolution? Filters and feature detection Pooling operations Part II: Adapting CNNs to Text (20 min) Text as sequence of embeddings 1D convolution over sequences Why CNNs make sense for language Part III: CNNs for Sentence Classification (35 min) Kim (2014): Convolutional Neural Networks for Sentence Classification Architecture details and worked examples Multiple filter sizes and max-pooling Part IV: Advanced Topics (10 min) Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 3/1 What is a Convolution? Intuition: Slide a small pattern detector (filter) over input Mathematical definition (1D): ∞ X (f ∗ g )[n] = f [m] · g [n − m] m=−∞ For discrete signals with finite support: (f ∗ g )[n] = k−1 X f [m] · g [n − m] m=0 In neural networks: f is the filter/kernel (learned parameters) g is the input (data) Output is feature map (activations) Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 4/1 Visual Example: Edge Detection Image: 2D grid of pixel values Filter: 3×3 kernel to detect vertical edges Input Output Filter 10 10 10 90 90 -1 0 1 10 10 10 90 90 -1 0 1 0 0 240 0 10 10 10 90 90 -1 0 1 0 0 240 0 10 10 10 90 90 High activation where vertical edge exists! Filter detects transition from dark (10) to bright (90) Maximum response at boundary Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 5/1 Convolution Operation: Step by Step 1D Example: Detect pattern in sequence [2, 3, 5, 1, 4, 6] Filter: [-1, 0, 1] (detects increasing patterns) Input: 2 3 5 1 4 6 Filter: [-1, 0, 1] (−1)(2) + (0)(3) + (1)(5) = 3 Output: 3 -2 3 5 Stride: How much we shift filter (typically 1) Padding: Add zeros at boundaries (to maintain size) Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 6/1 Key CNN Concepts 1. Local connectivity: Each output unit sees only small region of input Filter size: 3×3, 5×5, etc. Reduces parameters dramatically vs. fully connected 2. Parameter sharing: Same filter used across entire input Learn one pattern detector, apply everywhere E.g., 3×3 filter = 9 parameters for entire image 3. Translation invariance: Detect pattern regardless of position Edge detector works at any location Important for both images and text! Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 7/1 Multiple Filters and Channels Multiple filters detect different patterns: Filter 1: Vertical edges Filter 2: Horizontal edges Filter 3: Diagonal patterns Filter 4: Corners Output: Multiple feature maps (one per filter) Input: H × W × Cin (height × width × channels) Filters: k × k × Cin × Cout Output: H ′ × W ′ × Cout Stacking layers: Early layers: Simple patterns (edges) Middle layers: Parts (eyes, noses in vision) Deep layers: Complex objects (faces, cars) Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 8/1 Activation Functions After convolution, apply non-linearity: ReLU (most common): f (x) = max(0, x) Simple, fast to compute Helps with gradient flow Introduces non-linearity (enables learning complex functions) Full operation: h = ReLU(W ∗ x + b) where ∗ is convolution, W is filter, b is bias Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 9/1 Pooling Operations Goal: Downsample feature maps, reduce dimensionality Max pooling (most common): Take maximum value in each region Example: 2×2 max pooling with stride 2 Input 1 5 2 6 3 7 4 8 2 6 1 5 4 Output 8 max pool 2×2 3 7 8 7 8 7 Why pooling? Reduces computation Provides invariance to small translations Captures ”most important” features Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 10 / 1 Average Pooling Alternative: Take average instead of maximum Input Output 1 3 2 4avg pool 2×2 4 5 5 7 6 8 (1 + 3 + 5 + 7)/4 = 4, (2 + 4 + 6 + 8)/4 = 5 Max vs. Average: Max: Emphasizes strongest activations Average: Considers all activations equally Max is more common in practice Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 11 / 1 CNN Architecture Example (Vision) Classic architecture: LeNet-5 (LeCun et al. 1998) Input32×32 Conv28×28×6 Pool14×14×6 Conv10×10×16 Pool5×5×16 FC Pattern: Conv → ReLU → Pool → Conv → ReLU → Pool → FC → Output Key ideas: Spatial dimensions decrease (32→14→5) Depth (channels) increases (1→6→16) Finally: Flatten and use fully connected layers Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 12 / 1 Why CNNs for Text? Text seems sequential, not spatial... But: Local patterns matter! N-grams: ”not good”, ”very important”, ”ice cream” Phrases: ”New York”, ”machine learning” Syntax: ”did not”, ”would have” CNNs can detect these patterns: Filter size 2 → bigrams Filter size 3 → trigrams Filter size 4+ → longer phrases Advantages for text: Parallelizable (unlike RNNs) Fast training and inference Good at capturing local dependencies Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 13 / 1 Text as Matrix: Word Embeddings Represent sentence as matrix: Sentence: ”I love this movie” Word embeddings (e.g., 50-dimensional): ”I” → e1 ∈ R50 ”love” → e2 ∈ R50 ”this” → e3 ∈ R50 ”movie” → e4 ∈ R50 Sentence matrix: S ∈ R4×50 Rows: Words (sequence length n) Columns: Embedding dimensions (d) Shape: n × d Think of this as an ”image” where each word is a row of pixels Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 14 / 1 1D Convolution Over Text Filter: Height = window size, Width = embedding dimension Example: Filter size 3 (trigrams) Filter shape: 3 × d (covers 3 words, all dimensions) Slide vertically down the sentence At each position: compute dot product + bias → activation Filter (3×d) Feature I love this movie embedding dim (d) Output: Feature map capturing presence of trigram patterns Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 15 / 1 Convolution Details Input: Sentence matrix S ∈ Rn×d n = sentence length d = embedding dimension Filter: W ∈ Rh×d h = filter height (e.g., 3 for trigrams) d = embedding dimension (same as input) Convolution at position i: h−1 d−1 X X ci = ReLU( Wj,k · Si+j,k + b) j=0 k=0 Feature map: c = [c1 , c2 , . . . , cn−h+1 ] Length: n − h + 1 (with no padding) One value for each valid filter position Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 16 / 1 Multiple Filters Use many filters to detect different patterns: With m filters of size h × d: Each filter produces one feature map: c(1) , c(2) , . . . , c(m) Each feature map has length n − h + 1 Interpretation: Filter 1: Detects ”not [adjective]” patterns (negation) Filter 2: Detects ”very [adjective]” (intensification) Filter 3: Detects person names (capitalization patterns) ... Filters learn these patterns automatically during training! Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 17 / 1 Max-Over-Time Pooling Problem: Variable-length sentences → variable-length feature maps Solution: Max-over-time pooling For each feature map c = [c1 , c2 , . . . , cn−h+1 ]: c̃ = max(c) = max{c1 , c2 , . . . , cn−h+1 } Result: Single number (maximum activation) per filter Interpretation: ”Did this pattern appear anywhere in the sentence?” Captures most important feature regardless of position Creates fixed-size representation from variable-length input With m filters → m-dimensional vector for entire sentence Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 18 / 1 The Influential Paper Kim (2014): ”Convolutional Neural Networks for Sentence Classification” Task: Sentence-level classification Sentiment analysis: positive/negative movie reviews Question type classification Subjectivity detection Key contributions: Simple, effective architecture Multiple filter sizes (different n-gram lengths) Pre-trained word embeddings (word2vec) Various training strategies Impact: Over 10,000 citations, standard baseline for text classification Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 19 / 1 Kim CNN Architecture Sentence Feature maps Max-pool Convolution h=4 ! much very movie this love I h=3 n × d matrix h=2 Concat Softmax Key: Multiple filter sizes capture different n-gram lengths! Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 20 / 1 Architecture Details Input: Sentence with n words, embedding dimension d Sentence matrix: S ∈ Rn×d Convolutional layer: Multiple filter sizes Filter sizes: h ∈ {3, 4, 5} (trigrams, 4-grams, 5-grams) 100 filters of each size → 300 filters total Each filter: h × d parameters Pooling: Max-over-time pooling One value per filter Output: 300-dimensional vector Fully connected + Softmax: FC layer with dropout (0.5) Softmax over classes Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 21 / 1 Worked Example: Sentiment Classification Sentence: ”I love this movie” Task: Binary sentiment (positive/negative) Step 1: Embeddings Each word → 300-dim vector (word2vec) Matrix: 4 × 300 Step 2: Convolution with filter size 2 Filter covers ”I love” → compute activation c1 Slide to ”love this” → activation c2 Slide to ”this movie” → activation c3 Feature map: [c1 , c2 , c3 ] Suppose: c1 = 0.3, c2 = 0.8, c3 = 0.1 Max pool: max(0.3, 0.8, 0.1) = 0.8 Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 22 / 1 Worked Example (continued) Step 3: Multiple filters of size 2 100 filters of size 2, each produces one value after max-pooling: [filter1 : 0.8, filter2 : 0.3, . . . , filter100 : 0.5] Step 4: Repeat for filter sizes 3, 4 Filter size 3: ”I love this” → c1 ”love this movie” → c2 Max pool each of 100 filters Filter size 4: ”I love this movie” → c1 (only one position) Max pool each of 100 filters Step 5: Concatenate [100 from size 2] + [100 from size 3] + [100 from size 4] = 300-dim vector Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 23 / 1 Worked Example (continued) Step 6: Fully connected layer 300-dim vector → Dropout (0.5) → Linear → Softmax z = W · dropout(h) + b P(pos) = exp(zpos ) exp(zpos ) + exp(zneg ) Example output: P(positive) = 0.92 P(negative) = 0.08 Prediction: Positive The filter that detected ”love this” had high activation, contributing to positive classification! Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 24 / 1 What Do Filters Learn? Example learned patterns (from Kim’s experiments): Filter detecting negation (size 2): High activation for: ”not good”, ”not great”, ”not worth” This filter has negative weight → reduces positive score Filter detecting intensification (size 2): High activation for: ”very good”, ”highly recommend”, ”extremely well” Positive weight → increases positive score Filter detecting superlatives (size 3): ”one of the best”, ”one of the worst” Context-dependent weighting Filters automatically discover linguistically meaningful patterns! Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 25 / 1 Training Strategies Kim explored several variants: 1. CNN-rand: Random initialization Initialize word embeddings randomly Learn from scratch 2. CNN-static: Pre-trained, frozen Use word2vec embeddings Keep fixed during training 3. CNN-non-static: Pre-trained, fine-tuned Initialize with word2vec Update during training Best performance! 4. CNN-multichannel: Both static and non-static Two sets of embeddings One static, one fine-tuned Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 26 / 1 Results on Sentiment Analysis Dataset: Movie Review (MR) - binary sentiment Model Accuracy Naive Bayes (baseline) SVM with hand-crafted features CNN-rand CNN-static CNN-non-static CNN-multichannel 79.4% 79.4% 76.1% 81.0% 81.5% 81.1% Key findings: Pre-trained embeddings crucial (+5%) Fine-tuning helps slightly Simple architecture, strong performance Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 27 / 1 Regularization Techniques To prevent overfitting: 1. Dropout (p = 0.5): Applied before fully connected layer Randomly drop 50% of features during training Prevents co-adaptation 2. L2 regularization: Add λ2 ||w||2 to loss Prevents large weights 3. Max-norm constraint: Constrain ||w|| ≤ s s If exceeds, rescale: w ← ||w|| w Kim used s = 3 Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 28 / 1 Hyperparameters (Kim 2014) Standard settings: Parameter Value Embedding dimension Filter sizes Filters per size Dropout rate L2 constraint Mini-batch size Optimizer 300 (word2vec) 3, 4, 5 100 0.5 3 (max-norm) 50 Adadelta Note: Simple, few hyperparameters to tune! Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 29 / 1 Character-Level CNNs Alternative: Apply CNNs to character sequences Architecture (Zhang et al. 2015): Input: Character one-hot vectors Convolution over character sequence Multiple layers of conv + pooling Works without word embeddings! Advantages: No vocabulary limitation Captures morphology (prefixes, suffixes) Robust to misspellings Language-agnostic Disadvantages: Longer sequences (more computation) Generally lower accuracy than word-level Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 30 / 1 Character-Level Example Word: ”unhappiness” Character embeddings: Each character → small embedding (e.g., 15-dim) Sequence: [u, n, h, a, p, p, i, n, e, s, s] Matrix: 11 × 15 Convolutional filters: Size 3: Detects ”un-” (prefix), ”-ness” (suffix) Size 5: Detects ”happi” (stem) Size 7: Longer patterns Max pooling → Fixed-size character-level word representation Useful for morphologically rich languages! Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 31 / 1 Very Deep CNNs Question: Can we stack many convolutional layers? VGG-like architectures for text: Many small filters (size 3) stacked Receptive field grows: 3 → 5 → 7 → ... Deeper = more complex patterns Challenges: Vanishing gradients Overfitting on small text datasets Computational cost Solutions: Residual connections (ResNets) Batch normalization Large datasets (important!) Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 32 / 1 Dilated Convolutions Problem: Standard convolution has limited receptive field Dilated (Atrous) convolution: Skip positions in the input Dilation rate r : gaps between filter positions Example: r = 2 means skip every other position Input: Standard (rate=1) Dilated (rate=2) Benefit: Larger receptive field without more parameters Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 33 / 1 CNNs vs. RNNs for Text Parallelization Training speed Long-range deps Fixed-length output Best for Parameter sharing CNNs RNNs Fully parallel Fast Limited by filter size Yes (via pooling) Classification, short texts Across positions Sequential Slower Natural No Seq2seq, generation Across time When to use CNNs: Sentence/document classification When local patterns matter (n-grams) Need for speed When to use RNNs: Sequence generation Neural Networks for NLP Need to model long-distance Convolutional dependencies James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 34 / 1 Modern Use of CNNs in NLP CNNs are still used in modern NLP: 1. Hybrid architectures: CNN for character-level features + RNN for word-level Used in ELMo, some BERT variants 2. Fast baselines: Quick experiments before expensive models Production systems needing speed 3. Specific applications: Relation extraction (mention-level patterns) Event detection Text classification at scale 4. Components in larger models: Gated convolutional networks ConvS2S for machine translation Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 35 / 1 PyTorch Implementation: CNN Layer import torch import torch.nn as nn class TextCNN(nn.Module): def __init__(self, vocab_size, embed_dim, num_classes, filter_sizes=[3,4,5], num_filters=100): super().__init__() # Embedding layer self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, embed_dim) # Convolutional layers (one for each filter size) self.convs = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Conv2d(1, num_filters, (fs, embed_dim)) for fs in filter_sizes ]) # Fully connected layer Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 36 / 1 PyTorch Implementation: Forward Pass def forward(self, x): # x: (batch_size, seq_len) # Embedding: (batch_size, seq_len, embed_dim) embedded = self.embedding(x) # Add channel dimension: (batch_size, 1, seq_len, embed_dim) embedded = embedded.unsqueeze(1) # Apply convolutions and max-over-time pooling conv_outputs = [] for conv in self.convs: # Conv: (batch_size, num_filters, seq_len - fs + 1, 1) h = torch.relu(conv(embedded)) # Max pool: (batch_size, num_filters) h = torch.max(h, dim=2)[0].squeeze() conv_outputs.append(h) Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 37 / 1 Training Loop model = TextCNN(vocab_size=10000, embed_dim=300, num_classes=2) criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss() optimizer = torch.optim.Adadelta(model.parameters()) for epoch in range(num_epochs): for batch_x, batch_y in dataloader: # Forward pass outputs = model(batch_x) loss = criterion(outputs, batch_y) # Backward pass optimizer.zero_grad() loss.backward() # Gradient clipping (for max-norm constraint) torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 3.0) Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 38 / 1 Key Takeaways CNNs for Text: Apply convolution over word embeddings Detect local patterns (n-grams, phrases) Max-over-time pooling for fixed-size representation Kim (2014) Architecture: Multiple filter sizes (3, 4, 5) → different n-gram lengths Pre-trained embeddings crucial Simple but effective Advantages: Fast (parallelizable) Few hyperparameters Strong performance on classification Limitations: Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 39 / 1 CNNs in the Modern NLP Stack 2014-2016: CNNs popular for text classification 2016-2017: RNNs dominate sequence tasks 2017+: Attention and Transformers take over But CNNs still relevant: Character-level modeling Fast baselines Hybrid architectures Resource-constrained settings Conceptual importance: First successful deep learning for text Showed embeddings + simple architecture works Paved way for more complex models Understanding CNNs helps understand Transformers Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 40 / 1 Looking Ahead Next class: RNNs Sequential processing Hidden states and memory LSTMs and GRUs Better for variable-length outputs Connection: CNNs: Local patterns, parallel RNNs: Sequential dependencies, recurrent Both use embeddings Both addressed by Transformers (later) Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 41 / 1 Resources Key papers: Kim (2014): ”Convolutional Neural Networks for Sentence Classification” Zhang et al. (2015): ”Character-level Convolutional Networks for Text Classification” Kalchbrenner et al. (2014): ”A Convolutional Neural Network for Modelling Sentences” Implementations: PyTorch tutorials on text classification AllenNLP library (CNN text classifier) Keras/TensorFlow examples Further reading: Goodfellow et al., Deep Learning, Chapter 9 (CNNs) Stanford CS224N lecture notes on CNNs Convolutional Neural Networks for NLP James Pustejovsky March 10, 2026 42 / 1 Questions? Solution: Unroll the recurrence, then backprop Forward pass (left to right): h1 → h2 → h3 → · · · → hT Backward pass (right to left): ∂L ∂L ∂L → → ··· → ∂hT ∂hT −1 ∂h1 Key insight: Gradients flow backward through time Error at time T affects parameters used at all previous steps Need to accumulate gradients across time James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 12 / 44 BPTT: Mathematical Derivation Gradient of loss w.r.t. hidden state at time t: Direct contribution from output: ∂Lt ∂ht Contribution from future (via ht+1 ): ∂Lt ∂L ∂ht+1 ∂L = + ∂ht ∂ht ∂ht+1 ∂ht Since ht+1 = tanh(Whh ht + Wxh xt+1 + bh ): ∂ht+1 = diag(tanh′ (·))Whh ∂ht Recursive formula: James Pustejovsky ∂L ∂Lt ∂L T = + Whh diag(tanh′ (·)) ∂ht ∂ht ∂ht+1 Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 13 / 44 Gradient w.r.t. Recurrent Weights Total gradient for Whh : Must accumulate contributions from all time steps: T X ∂L ∂ht ∂L = ∂Whh ∂ht ∂Whh t=1 where: ∂ht = diag(tanh′ (·))hT t−1 ∂Whh Similarly for other parameters: PT ∂L ′ ∂L T t=1 ∂ht diag(tanh (·))xt ∂Wxh = PT ∂Lt T ∂L t=1 ∂yt ht ∂Why = Parameter sharing means gradients accumulate across all time steps! James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 14 / 44 Truncated BPTT Problem: For long sequences, BPTT is expensive Memory: Must store all hidden states Computation: Gradients propagate through entire sequence Solution: Truncate backpropagation after k steps Algorithm: 1 Forward pass: Process entire sequence as normal 2 Backward pass: Only backprop k steps into the past 3 Next batch: Continue from last hidden state (detached) Trade-off: Constant memory and computation Cannot learn dependencies longer than k steps Common: k = 20 to 50 James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 15 / 44 Long-Range Dependencies Consider: ”The cat, which was very hungry and had been wandering in the rain all day, was tired” To predict ”was” (singular), must remember ”cat” (singular subject) from 14 words earlier Question: Can RNNs learn such dependencies? Problem: Vanishing gradients Gradients must propagate backward through many time steps Each step involves multiplication by Whh and tanh′ Gradients shrink exponentially with distance James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 16 / 44 Vanishing Gradient: Mathematical Analysis Gradient of loss at time T w.r.t. hidden state at time t: T ∂LT ∂LT Y ∂hk = ∂ht ∂hT ∂hk−1 k=t+1 = T ∂LT Y T Whh diag(tanh′ (zk )) ∂hT k=t+1 Key observations: Product of T − t Jacobian matrices T diag(tanh′ (·)) Each Jacobian: Whh tanh′ (z) ≤ 1, often ≪ 1 for large |z| T diag(tanh′ (·))|| < 1: Result: If ||Whh James Pustejovsky || ∂LT Recurrent Neural Networks || ≈ γ T −t →0 as forTNLP −t →∞ March 12, 2026 17 / 44 Exploding Gradients Opposite problem: If ||Whh || > 1: || ∂LT || ≈ γ T −t → ∞ ∂ht Consequences: Gradients become extremely large Parameter updates overshoot Training becomes unstable (NaN values) Solution: Gradient clipping g← ( g θ ||g|| g if ||g|| ≤ θ otherwise Typical threshold: θ = 5 or 10 Exploding gradients are easier to fix than vanishing gradients! James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 18 / 44 Why Vanishing Gradients Matter Practical consequences: 1. Cannot learn long-term dependencies Gradient signal from distant past is too weak RNN ”forgets” information after 10 steps Subject-verb agreement: ”The key to the cabinets is/are on the table” 2. Slow learning Early layers receive negligible gradients Parameters don’t update effectively 3. Mode collapse Network learns to ignore distant context Relies only on recent words This motivated development of LSTMs and GRUs! James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 19 / 44 LSTM: Motivation Goal: Maintain long-term dependencies without vanishing gradients Key innovation (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber 1997): Introduce cell state ct : ”memory highway” Use gates to control information flow Additive updates to cell state (not multiplicative!) Three gates: 1 Forget gate ft : What to remove from memory 2 Input gate it : What new information to store 3 Output gate ot : What to output from memory Gates are learned functions that output values in [0, 1] James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 20 / 44 LSTM Equations Gate computations (all use sigmoid σ): ft = σ(Wf [ht−1 , xt ] + bf ) (forget) it = σ(Wi [ht−1 , xt ] + bi ) (input) ot = σ(Wo [ht−1 , xt ] + bo ) (output) Cell candidate (uses tanh): c̃t = tanh(Wc [ht−1 , xt ] + bc ) Cell state update (element-wise operations): ct = ft ⊙ ct−1 + it ⊙ c̃t Hidden state (output): ht = ot ⊙ tanh(ct ) Notation: [ht−1 , xt ] is concatenation, ⊙ is element-wise multiplication James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 21 / 44 LSTM: Intuitive Understanding Cell state ct : The ”conveyor belt” Information flows with minimal transformation Enables gradient flow over long sequences Forget gate ft : ”What to erase?” ft = 0: Completely forget ct−1 ft = 1: Fully retain ct−1 Example: Forget previous subject when new sentence starts Input gate it : ”What new information to add?” Controls how much of c̃t enters cell state Example: Remember new subject when encountered Output gate ot : ”What to expose?” Filters cell state for current prediction Example: Output relevant features for current word prediction James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural high: Store ”singular” in ct Forget gate ft erases previous number info At ”on the” (irrelevant words): Forget gate ft ≈ 1: Keep number info in memory Input gate it ≈ 0: Don’t add new info At ”sits” (verb): Output gate ot is high: Expose number from ct Helps predict singular verb form James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 23 / 44 Why LSTMs Solve Vanishing Gradients Gradient flow through cell state: ∂ct = ft ∂ct−1 Contrast with vanilla RNN: ∂ht T = Whh diag(tanh′ (·)) ∂ht−1 Key difference: LSTM: Gradient flows through addition and element-wise multiplication by forget gate Vanilla RNN: Gradient flows through matrix multiplication and tanh derivative Result: If ft ≈ 1: Gradient flows unimpeded (like residual connection) No repeated matrix multiplications → no × ht [ht−1 , xt ] Flow: Cell state (red) is modified by forget gate (×) and input gate (+) James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 25 / 44 GRU: Simplified LSTM Motivation (Cho et al. 2014): LSTMs work well but have many parameters Can we simplify while maintaining performance? Key simplifications: Merge cell state and hidden state Two gates instead of three (update and reset) Fewer parameters → faster training GRU equations: zt = σ(Wz [ht−1 , xt ]) (update gate) rt = σ(Wr [ht−1 , xt ]) (reset gate) h̃t = tanh(Wh [rt ⊙ ht−1 , xt ]) ht = (1 − zt ) ⊙ ht−1 + zt ⊙ h̃t James Pustejovsky (candidate) (new hidden) Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 26 / 44 GRU Intuition Update gate zt : ”How much to update?” zt = 0: Keep old state ht−1 (like LSTM forget gate = 1) zt = 1: Use new candidate h̃t (like LSTM input gate = 1) Interpolation between old and new Reset gate rt : ”How much past to use?” rt = 0: Ignore previous hidden state when computing candidate rt = 1: Use full previous hidden state Allows model to drop irrelevant history Final update: Linear interpolation ht = (1 − zt ) ⊙ ht−1 + zt ⊙ h̃t If zt = 1 everywhere: full update. If zt = 0: no change. James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 27 / 44 LSTM vs. GRU Gates State Parameters Gradient flow Performance Training speed LSTM GRU 3 (forget, input, output) Separate ct and ht More Through cell state Slight edge on some tasks Slower 2 (update, reset) Single ht Fewer ( 25% less) Through hidden state Comparable Faster In practice: Both work well for most NLP tasks LSTM: Slight advantage on tasks requiring long memory GRU: Faster, simpler, good default choice Try both and see what works best James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 28 / 44 Motivation: Context from Both Directions Problem with standard RNNs: Only see past context (left-to-right) Cannot see future words Example: ”I arrived at the bank after crossing the ” To disambiguate ”bank”: Need to see ”river” (if it appears later) Or ”street” (then financial institution) Solution: Bidirectional RNN (Schuster & Paliwal 1997) Process sequence both left-to-right AND right-to-left Combine information from both directions Get full context for each position James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 29 / 44 Bidirectional RNN Architecture Two separate RNNs: Forward RNN (⃗ht ): ⃗ht = RNNfwd (xt , ⃗ht−1 ) Backward RNN (ht ): ht = RNNbwd (xt , ht+1 ) Combine (typically concatenation): ht = [⃗ht ; h ] t t t 5 Linear + softmax: Predict POS tag for each word At position 3 (”sat”): ⃗h3 knows ”The cat” came before h3 knows ”on the mat” comes after Combined: Can better disambiguate as VERB (not NOUN) BiLSTMs are standard for sequence labeling tasks! T 1 X log P(xt | x<t ) PPL = exp − T t=1 Lower perplexity = better model James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 32 / 44 Generating Text from RNN Sampling procedure: 1 2 Initialize with start token: x1 = ⟨START⟩ For t = 1, 2, 3, . . .: Compute ht = RNN(xt , ht−1 ) Get distribution: P(xt+1 | x≤t ) = softmax(Why ht ) Sample: xt+1 ∼ P(xt+1 | x≤t ) 3 Stop when xt+1 = ⟨END⟩ or max length reached Sampling strategies: Greedy: xt+1 = arg max P(xt+1 | x≤t ) Random sampling: Sample from full distribution Top-k sampling: Sample from top k most likely words ) Temperature: PT (x) = Pexp(z/T exp(z ′ /T ) (T ¿ 1: more random) James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 33 / 44 Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) Architecture (Sutskever et al. 2014): Encoder: Process input sequence → fixed-size context vector Input: English sentence RNN produces hidden states h1 , . . . , hT Context: c = hT (final hidden state) Decoder: Generate output sequence from context Initialize with context: s0 = c At each step: st = RNN(yt−1 , st−1 ) Output: P(yt | y<t , c) = softmax(Ws st ) Training: Teacher forcing Use gold target yt−1 as input (not model’s prediction) Speeds up training, prevents error accumulation James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 34 / 44 Seq2Seq Example: Machine Translation Input: ”The cat sat on the mat” Output: ”Le chat était assis sur le tapis” Encoder: Process English words left-to-right h1 (The), h2 (cat), ..., h6 (mat) Final state h6 = sentence representation Decoder: Initialize: s0 = h6 Generate: ⟨START⟩ → ”Le” → ”chat” → ”était” → ... Each word conditioned on context + previous French words Challenge: Everything compressed into single vector h6 ! This limitation motivated attention mechanisms (next lecture) James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 35 / 44 Named Entity Recognition with BiLSTM Task: Label each word with entity type Example: ”Barack Obama visited Microsoft” Labels: B-PER I-PER O B-ORG Architecture: 1 Word embeddings: 300-dim vectors 2 BiLSTM: Forward and backward, hidden dim = 256 3 Concatenate: h = [⃗ ht ; ht ] ∈ R512 t 4 Linear + softmax: 512 → 9 classes (B-/I-/O for PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) 5 Optional: CRF layer on top for label dependencies Why BiLSTM helps: ”Obama” benefits from seeing both ”Barack” (before) and ”visited” (after) Disambiguates: ”Washington” (person vs. location) based on context James Pustejovsky Recurrent Neural Networks for NLP March 12, 2026 36 / 44 Training Tips 1. Gradient clipping: Essential for RNNs Clip by norm: threshold = 5-10 2. Initialization: Recurrent weights: Orthogonal initialization Input weights: Xavier/Glorot Biases: Usually zero (LSTM forget bias → 1) 3. Optimization: Adam works well Learning rate: 0.001-0.01 (tune) Learning rate decay: Reduce by 0.5-0.8 when plateaus 4.
