text: Self-Attention & Transformers Key Concepts & Worked Examples COSI 115b — Spring 2026 Recitation 1 / 34 Today’s Roadmap 1 Self-attention — the core mechanism: queries, keys, values 2 Multi-head attention — why one head isn’t enough 3 Positional encodings — why Transformers need them 4 Decoder architecture — how GPT-2 puts it all together These ideas are the foundation of the new assignment, which is up on Moodle now (due April 17). 2 / 34 Self-Attention The core mechanism 3 / 34 Self-Attention: The Core Equations Given a query q ∈ Rd , keys {k1 , . . . , kn }, and values {v1 , . . . , vn }: Attention Output c= n X vi αi i=1 Attention Weights exp(ki⊤ q) αi = Pn ⊤ j=1 exp(kj q) Key intuition: c is a weighted average of value vectors, where the weights come from how well each key matches the query. 4 / 34 Quick Check: Understanding the Basics Question 1: What is the range of each αi ? Can αi ever be exactly 0 or exactly 1? 5 / 34 Quick Check: Understanding the Basics Question 1: What is the range of each αi ? Can αi ever be exactly 0 or exactly 1? P Each αi ∈ (0, 1), and i αi = 1. Strictly positive because exp(·) > 0. Never exactly 0 or 1, only approaches them in the limit. Question 2: What would c look like if all αi = 1/n? 5 / 34 Quick Check: Understanding the Basics Question 1: What is the range of each αi ? Can αi ever be exactly 0 or exactly 1? P Each αi ∈ (0, 1), and i αi = 1. Strictly positive because exp(·) > 0. Never exactly 0 or 1, only approaches them in the limit. Question 2: What would c look like if all αi = 1/n? P c = n1 ni=1 vi — the unweighted average of all values. This is the “no preference” case where the query matches all keys equally. 5 / 34 What Does the Dot Product ki⊤ q Tell Us? Recall the geometric form: ki⊤ q = ∥ki ∥ ∥q∥ cos θ The score depends on two things: 1 Direction: How aligned are ki and q? (cos θ) 2 Magnitude: How large are ∥ki ∥ and ∥q∥? Both matter! A key can get a high score by being well-aligned with the query, or simply by having a large norm. 6 / 34 Copying in Attention Question: If one key kj is perfectly aligned with q and all other keys are orthogonal to q, what does c look like? 7 / 34 Copying in Attention Question: If one key kj is perfectly aligned with q and all other keys are orthogonal to q, what does c look like? The aligned key gets score ∥kj ∥ ∥q∥ > 0. All others get score 0. After softmax: αj = e ∥kj ∥∥q∥ ∥k ∥∥q∥ e j +(n−1) e0 |{z} =1 7 / 34 Copying in Attention Question: If one key kj is perfectly aligned with q and all other keys are orthogonal to q, what does c look like? The aligned key gets score ∥kj ∥ ∥q∥ > 0. All others get score 0. After softmax: αj = e ∥kj ∥∥q∥ ∥k ∥∥q∥ e j +(n−1) e0 |{z} =1 For large ∥q∥, this approaches 1. So: c ≈ vj The attention mechanism copies value vj to the output! Follow-up: What if we want to attend to two keys equally? Can we do that? 7 / 34 Softmax Temperature: Controlling Sharpness The attention scores si = ki⊤ q go through softmax. What if we scale them? exp(β si ) αi = P j exp(β sj ) Question: What happens as β gets very large? Very small? 8 / 34 Softmax Temperature: Controlling Sharpness The attention scores si = ki⊤ q go through softmax. What if we scale them? exp(β si ) αi = P j exp(β sj ) Question: What happens as β gets very large? Very small? β → ∞: distribution becomes peaked (approaches one-hot at the max) β → 0: distribution becomes uniform (αi ≈ 1/n) β = 1: standard softmax 8 / 34 Softmax Temperature: Controlling Sharpness The attention scores si = ki⊤ q go through softmax. What if we scale them? exp(β si ) αi = P j exp(β sj ) Question: What happens as β gets very large? Very small? β → ∞: distribution becomes peaked (approaches one-hot at the max) β → 0: distribution becomes uniform (αi ≈ 1/n) β = 1: standard softmax Key observation: Multiplying q by a scalar β is the same as scaling all scores by β. So the norm of the query controls how “decisive” the attention is. 8 / 34 Example: Scores [1, 1, 0] at Different Temperatures Suppose three keys have scores s1 = 1, s2 = 1, s3 = 0. Question: What are the attention weights at β = 1? 9 / 34 Example: Scores [1, 1, 0] at Different Temperatures Suppose three keys have scores s1 = 1, s2 = 1, s3 = 0. Question: What are the attention weights at β = 1? β 1 α1 0.42 α2 0.42 α3 0.16 9 / 34 Example: Scores [1, 1, 0] at Different Temperatures Suppose three keys have scores s1 = 1, s2 = 1, s3 = 0. Question: What are the attention weights at β = 1? β 1 10 100 α1 0.42 ≈ 0.50 ≈ 0.50 α2 0.42 ≈ 0.50 ≈ 0.50 α3 0.16 ≈0 ≈0 At β = 1: the third key (score 0) still gets 16% of the weight! At β = 10: it’s essentially ignored. The two tied leaders split evenly. 9 / 34 Example: Scores [1, 1, 0] at Different Temperatures Suppose three keys have scores s1 = 1, s2 = 1, s3 = 0. Question: What are the attention weights at β = 1? β 1 10 100 α1 0.42 ≈ 0.50 ≈ 0.50 α2 0.42 ≈ 0.50 ≈ 0.50 α3 0.16 ≈0 ≈0 At β = 1: the third key (score 0) still gets 16% of the weight! At β = 10: it’s essentially ignored. The two tied leaders split evenly. Takeaway: You can make attention selective by scaling up the query. But even equal scores don’t give exactly 21 — the non-max entries always dilute. 9 / 34 Orthogonal Keys: A Clean Setting A useful special case: keys are orthonormal. ki⊤ kj = 0 for i ̸= j ∥ki ∥ = 1 (orthogonal) (unit norm) If you build q as a linear combination of some keys, the dot products are easy to compute. Exercise: Let q = 3k1 + 3k2 , with 4 orthonormal keys. What is k1⊤ q? What is k3⊤ q? 10 / 34 Orthogonal Keys: A Clean Setting A useful special case: keys are orthonormal. ki⊤ kj = 0 for i ̸= j ∥ki ∥ = 1 (orthogonal) (unit norm) If you build q as a linear combination of some keys, the dot products are easy to compute. Exercise: Let q = 3k1 + 3k2 , with 4 orthonormal keys. What is k1⊤ q? What is k3⊤ q? k1⊤ q = 3 k1⊤ k1 +3 k1⊤ k2 = 3 | {z } | {z } =1 =0 k3⊤ q = 3 k3⊤ k1 +3 k3⊤ k2 = 0 | {z } | {z } =0 =0 10 / 34 Orthogonal Keys: Attention Weights So the scores are [3, 3, 0, 0]. Question: After softmax, do keys 1 and 2 get exactly 12 each? 11 / 34 Orthogonal Keys: Attention Weights So the scores are [3, 3, 0, 0]. Question: After softmax, do keys 1 and 2 get exactly 12 each? 3 20.09 No! α1 = α2 = 2e 3e+2e 0 = 2(20.09)+2 ≈ 0.475. Keys 3 and 4 still get ≈ 0.025 each. Not negligible! Question: How could we make keys 1 and 2 dominate more? 11 / 34 Orthogonal Keys: Attention Weights So the scores are [3, 3, 0, 0]. Question: After softmax, do keys 1 and 2 get exactly 12 each? 3 20.09 No! α1 = α2 = 2e 3e+2e 0 = 2(20.09)+2 ≈ 0.475. Keys 3 and 4 still get ≈ 0.025 each. Not negligible! Question: How could we make keys 1 and 2 dominate more? Scale up! Use q = 30(k1 + k2 ) instead of 3(k1 + k2 ). Scores become [30, 30, 0, 0], and the softmax concentrates almost entirely on keys 1 and 2. Takeaway: With orthonormal keys, linear combinations give precise control over scores, and scaling controls selectivity. 11 / 34 What Happens When Keys Are Noisy? In practice, keys are computed by a neural network — they’re noisy. Model this as: ki ∼ N (µi , Σi ), where µi are orthonormal means. Two noise models: 1 2 Isotropic: Σi = αI (tiny, equal noise in all directions). Keys stay close to their means. Anisotropic: Σa = αI + 12 µa µ⊤ a (large noise along µa ). Key ka points in roughly the right direction, but its magnitude varies a lot. Question: Under isotropic noise, does your carefully designed query still work? Why? 12 / 34 What Happens When Keys Are Noisy? In practice, keys are computed by a neural network — they’re noisy. Model this as: ki ∼ N (µi , Σi ), where µi are orthonormal means. Two noise models: 1 2 Isotropic: Σi = αI (tiny, equal noise in all directions). Keys stay close to their means. Anisotropic: Σa = αI + 12 µa µ⊤ a (large noise along µa ). Key ka points in roughly the right direction, but its magnitude varies a lot. Question: Under isotropic noise, does your carefully designed query still work? Why? Yes — tiny noise in all directions barely changes any dot product. The scores stay close to their noiseless values. 12 / 34 Visualizing Anisotropic Noise ka (large norm) µa high variance along µa ka (small norm) Direction is roughly preserved, but the magnitude fluctuates. Question: If your query has a component along µa , what happens to ka⊤ q across different samples? 13 / 34 Visualizing Anisotropic Noise ka (large norm) µa high variance along µa ka (small norm) Direction is roughly preserved, but the magnitude fluctuates. Question: If your query has a component along µa , what happens to ka⊤ q across different samples? It fluctuates a lot — the score is proportional to ∥ka ∥, which has high variance. So αa and therefore c become unstable. 13 / 34 Noise Direction Matters! ⊤ We said ka = µa + ϵ, so ka⊤ q = µ⊤ a q + ϵ q. The noise contribution to the score is ϵ⊤ q. Question: When does this noise term cause big problems? When is it harmless? 14 / 34 Noise Direction Matters! ⊤ We said ka = µa + ϵ, so ka⊤ q = µ⊤ a q + ϵ q. The noise contribution to the score is ϵ⊤ q. Question: When does this noise term cause big problems? When is it harmless? Big problems: when ϵ is aligned with q — then ϵ⊤ q is large and fluctuating. Harmless: when ϵ is orthogonal to q — then ϵ⊤ q ≈ 0 regardless of ∥ϵ∥. 14 / 34 Noise Direction Matters! ⊤ We said ka = µa + ϵ, so ka⊤ q = µ⊤ a q + ϵ q. The noise contribution to the score is ϵ⊤ q. Question: When does this noise term cause big problems? When is it harmless? Big problems: when ϵ is aligned with q — then ϵ⊤ q is large and fluctuating. Harmless: when ϵ is orthogonal to q — then ϵ⊤ q ≈ 0 regardless of ∥ϵ∥. The punchline: It’s not just about how much noise there is, but what direction it’s in relative to the query. This will be important when we compare single-head vs. multi-head attention. 14 / 34 Multi-Head Attention Why one head isn’t enough 15 / 34 The Problem With a Single Query Suppose we want c ≈ 12 (va + vb ) — an equal mix of two values. With one query, you need to attend to both keys simultaneously. This means q must have components along both µa and µb . Question: If ka has high variance along µa , and your single query q has a component along µa (which it must, to attend to a), what goes wrong? 16 / 34 The Problem With a Single Query Suppose we want c ≈ 12 (va + vb ) — an equal mix of two values. With one query, you need to attend to both keys simultaneously. This means q must have components along both µa and µb . Question: If ka has high variance along µa , and your single query q has a component along µa (which it must, to attend to a), what goes wrong? The score ka⊤ q fluctuates wildly. Sometimes αa ≫ αb (over-attend to a), sometimes αa ≪ αb (under-attend to a). The output c has high variance — not reliably 12 (va + vb ). 16 / 34 Multi-Head Attention: Split the Work Multi-head (simplified, 2 heads): Head 1 uses query q1 → produces c1 Head 2 uses query q2 → produces c2 Final output: c = 12 (c1 + c2 ) Key idea: Each head can specialize. Head 1 focuses on va alone. Head 2 focuses on vb alone. Question: If ka is noisy along µa , which head is affected? Which head is safe? 17 / 34 Multi-Head Attention: Split the Work Multi-head (simplified, 2 heads): Head 1 uses query q1 → produces c1 Head 2 uses query q2 → produces c2 Final output: c = 12 (c1 + c2 ) Key idea: Each head can specialize. Head 1 focuses on va alone. Head 2 focuses on vb alone. Question: If ka is noisy along µa , which head is affected? Which head is safe? Head 1 (query aligned with µa , attending to a): affected Head 2 (query aligned with µb , attending to b): safe — the noise is orthogonal to its query! 17 / 34 Multi-Head Attention: Split the Work Multi-head (simplified, 2 heads): Head 1 uses query q1 → produces c1 Head 2 uses query q2 → produces c2 Final output: c = 12 (c1 + c2 ) Key idea: Each head can specialize. Head 1 focuses on va alone. Head 2 focuses on vb alone. Question: If ka is noisy along µa , which head is affected? Which head is safe? Head 1 (query aligned with µa , attending to a): affected Head 2 (query aligned with µb , attending to b): safe — the noise is orthogonal to its query! Only half the output is noisy ⇒ lower overall variance. 17 / 34 Why Is Head 2 Safe? A Closer Look ka ’s noise is along µa . Head 2’s query is along µb . Question: What is ka⊤ q2 when the noise is along µa and q2 is along µb ? 18 / 34 Why Is Head 2 Safe? A Closer Look ka ’s noise is along µa . Head 2’s query is along µb . Question: What is ka⊤ q2 when the noise is along µa and q2 is along µb ? ka⊤ q2 = (µa + ϵ)⊤ q2 = µ⊤ q | a{z }2 ≈ 0 (orthogonal) + ϵ⊤ q2 | {z } ≈ 0 (noise ⊥ query) The noisy key ka gets a near-zero score in head 2, regardless of its norm. Head 2 is insulated from the noise. Question: If we used the same query for both heads (q1 = q2 ), would we still get this benefit? 18 / 34 Why Is Head 2 Safe? A Closer Look ka ’s noise is along µa . Head 2’s query is along µb . Question: What is ka⊤ q2 when the noise is along µa and q2 is along µb ? ka⊤ q2 = (µa + ϵ)⊤ q2 = µ⊤ q | a{z }2 ≈ 0 (orthogonal) + ϵ⊤ q2 | {z } ≈ 0 (noise ⊥ query) The noisy key ka gets a near-zero score in head 2, regardless of its norm. Head 2 is insulated from the noise. Question: If we used the same query for both heads (q1 = q2 ), would we still get this benefit? No! Both heads would suffer from the same noise. You’d just be averaging two copies of the same noisy output. The benefit comes from using different queries. 18 / 34 Positional Encodings Why word order matters 19 / 34 The Transformer’s Symmetry Problem Consider the Transformer’s two core operations: 1 Self-attention: Computes Q, K, V from input X, applies softmax. 2 Feed-forward: Applied independently to each position (row of H). Thought experiment: What happens if we shuffle the input tokens? Represent shuffling as Xperm = PX, where P is a permutation matrix. Question: Compute Qperm = Xperm WQ . Can you factor out P? 20 / 34 The Transformer’s Symmetry Problem Consider the Transformer’s two core operations: 1 Self-attention: Computes Q, K, V from input X, applies softmax. 2 Feed-forward: Applied independently to each position (row of H). Thought experiment: What happens if we shuffle the input tokens? Represent shuffling as Xperm = PX, where P is a permutation matrix. Question: Compute Qperm = Xperm WQ . Can you factor out P? Qperm = PXWQ = PQ. Yes — P just passes through the linear projection. Same for K and V: Kperm = PK, Vperm = PV. 20 / 34 Chasing P Through Attention We have Qp = PQ, Kp = PK, Vp = PV. ⊤ Question: What is Qp K⊤ p ? Each token’s representation is the same regardless of position. Question: Why is this a problem for language? Can you think of a concrete example? 22 / 34 Permutation Equivariance Tracing through the full model (attention + feed-forward): Zperm = PZ Shuffling the input just shuffles the output. Each token’s representation is the same regardless of position. Question: Why is this a problem for language? Can you think of a concrete example? “The dog bit the man” and “The man bit the dog” contain the same tokens. A permutation-equivariant model produces the same representations (just reordered) for both — it can’t distinguish their meanings. Question: How could we break this symmetry? 22 / 34 Permutation Equivariance Tracing through the full model (attention + feed-forward): Zperm = PZ Shuffling the input just shuffles the output. Each token’s representation is the same regardless of position. Question: Why is this a problem for language? Can you think of a concrete example? “The dog bit the man” and “The man bit the dog” contain the same tokens. A permutation-equivariant model produces the same representations (just reordered) for both — it can’t distinguish their meanings. Question: How could we break this symmetry? Add position-dependent information to the input! If each position has a unique “stamp,” shuffling changes what the model sees. 22 / 34 Permutation Matrices: Quick Refresher A permutation matrix P ∈ RT ×T reorders rows:   0 1 0 P = 0 0 1 1 0 0 ⇒   row 2 of X PX = row 3 of X row 1 of X Key properties: P is orthogonal: P⊤ P = PP⊤ = I softmax(PAP⊤ ) = P softmax(A) P⊤ ReLU(PA) = P ReLU(A) Question: If 1 is a column vector of all ones, what is P1? 23 / 34 Permutation Matrices: Quick Refresher A permutation matrix P ∈ RT ×T reorders rows:   0 1 0 P = 0 0 1 1 0 0 ⇒   row 2 of X PX = row 3 of X row 1 of X Key properties: P is orthogonal: P⊤ P = PP⊤ = I softmax(PAP⊤ ) = P softmax(A) P⊤ ReLU(PA) = P ReLU(A) Question: If 1 is a column vector of all ones, what is P1? P1 = 1. Permuting a vector of all ones just gives all ones again. (This comes up when tracing P through the feed-forward bias terms.) 23 / 34 Sinusoidal Positional Encodings Solution: Add a position-dependent vector to each token embedding. Xpos = X + Φ where Φ ∈ RT ×d encodes positions using sines and cosines:     t t Φ(t, 2i) = sin , Φ(t, 2i+1) = cos 100002i/d 100002i/d Each dimension oscillates at a different frequency: Low i ⇒ high frequency (changes rapidly with position) High i ⇒ low frequency (changes slowly) The result: every position gets a unique “fingerprint” of sines and cosines. 24 / 34 Why Do Positional Encodings Fix the Problem? Without Φ: permuting input X gives permuted output PZ. No position info. With Φ: the model sees X + Φ, not just X. Question: If we shuffle the tokens, the model receives PX + Φ. For the old equivariance to hold, we’d need PX + PΦ. Are these the same? 25 / 34 Why Do Positional Encodings Fix the Problem? Without Φ: permuting input X gives permuted output PZ. No position info. With Φ: the model sees X + Φ, not just X. Question: If we shuffle the tokens, the model receives PX + Φ. For the old equivariance to hold, we’d need PX + PΦ. Are these the same? No! PΦ ̸= Φ because different positions have different encodings. Permuting the position encodings changes them, but the model always uses the fixed Φ. So the model sees genuinely different inputs for different orderings — symmetry is broken. Question: Could two different positions t1 ̸= t2 ever have the same encoding Φ(t1 , :) = Φ(t2 , :)? 25 / 34 Why Do Positional Encodings Fix the Problem? Without Φ: permuting input X gives permuted output PZ. No position info. With Φ: the model sees X + Φ, not just X. Question: If we shuffle the tokens, the model receives PX + Φ. For the old equivariance to hold, we’d need PX + PΦ. Are these the same? No! PΦ ̸= Φ because different positions have different encodings. Permuting the position encodings changes them, but the model always uses the fixed Φ. So the model sees genuinely different inputs for different orderings — symmetry is broken. Question: Could two different positions t1 ̸= t2 ever have the same encoding Φ(t1 , :) = Φ(t2 , :)? Not for practical sequence lengths. Individual dimensions repeat (sine is periodic), but the combination of all dimensions at different incommensurable frequencies doesn’t. The lowest-frequency period is ≈ 62,832 — far longer than any practical sequence. 25 / 34 Position Encoding: Intuition Check Question: Suppo

text: An Introduction to Reinforcement Learning CS115B – Spring 2026 James Pustejovsky Why an RL lecture in CS115 ▶ RL is one of the main paradigms for learning from interaction rather than static labels. ▶ It gives students the vocabulary behind policies, rewards, trajectories, exploration, credit assignment, and planning. ▶ That vocabulary later appears in modern NLP and LLM post-training: RLHF, PPO, reward models, bandits, online learning, and preference optimization. ▶ Today we focus on general RL, not just LLMs. Big picture Supervised learning asks “what is the right output?”; RL asks “what sequence of actions leads to high long-term return?” 2 / 25 Where RL fits among learning paradigms Supervised ▶ Input-output pairs ▶ Immediate labels ▶ Independent examples Unsupervised / self-supervised Reinforcement learning ▶ Agent acts in an ▶ Structure in raw data environment ▶ No explicit reward ▶ Representation learning ▶ Receives rewards ▶ Must optimize long-term outcomes Delayed consequences are the core difficulty in RL. 3 / 25 The interaction loop state st policy action at environment reward rt+1 next state st+1 A trajectory is a sequence (s0 , a0 , r1 , s1 , a1 , r2 , . . . ). The learner wants to choose actions so that accumulated reward is large. 4 / 25 Reward, return, and the discount factor ▶ Reward rt+1 : immediate scalar feedback. ▶ Return Gt : total future reward from time t onward. Gt = rt+1 + γrt+2 + γ 2 rt+3 + · · · ▶ γ ∈ [0, 1) is the discount factor. ▶ Smaller γ: more myopic behavior. ▶ Larger γ: more emphasis on long-term consequences. Interpretation Discounting can encode uncertainty, finite attention horizon, or simply make the infinite sum well behaved. 5 / 25 MDPs and Value Functions Markov decision processes (MDPs) An RL task is often modeled as an MDP with: ▶ states S ▶ actions A ▶ transition dynamics P(s ′ | s, a) ▶ reward function R(s, a, s ′ ) ▶ discount factor γ Markov property The next state depends on the current state and action, not on the full earlier history. If the agent cannot observe the full state, we move toward partial observability (POMDPs), where memory becomes important. 6 / 25 MDPs and Value Functions Policies: how the agent acts ▶ A policy tells the agent what action to take. ▶ Deterministic policy: a = π(s) ▶ Stochastic policy: π(a | s) gives a distribution over actions. Why stochastic policies? ▶ exploration ▶ robustness ▶ natural fit for policy gradients In NLP/LLMs A language model already defines a token distribution, so stochastic policies feel natural. 7 / 25 MDPs and Value Functions State-value and action-value functions For a policy π: V π (s) = Eπ [Gt | st = s] Q π (s, a) = Eπ [Gt | st = s, at = a] ▶ V π (s): how good it is to be in state s. ▶ Q π (s, a): how good it is to take action a in state s. ▶ Optimal values define the best achievable long-term return. V ∗ (s) = max V π (s), π Q ∗ (s, a) = max Q π (s, a) π 8 / 25 MDPs and Value Functions Bellman equations Bellman expectation equation V π (s) = X π(a | s) X   P(s ′ , r | s, a) r + γV π (s ′ ) s ′ ,r a Bellman optimality equation V ∗ (s) = max a X   P(s ′ , r | s, a) r + γV ∗ (s ′ ) s ′ ,r ▶ These equations express a recursive decomposition of long-term value. ▶ Nearly every major RL algorithm is a way of exploiting this recursion. 9 / 25 MDPs and Value Functions The exploration-exploitation dilemma Exploit Explore Choose the action that currently looks best. Try actions that may reveal better long-term strategies. ▶ Too little exploration → stuck with mediocre behavior. ▶ Too much exploration → poor short-term performance. ▶ This issue already appears in the simpler multi-armed bandit setting. 10 / 25 MDPs and Value Functions Credit assignment and sparse rewards ▶ A reward may arrive long after the actions that caused it. ▶ Many tasks have sparse rewards: feedback appears only occasionally. ▶ Example: in a long dialogue, which earlier turn caused the final success or failure? action 1 action 2 action 3 action 4 reward at end Value functions and return estimates help propagate delayed reward backward through time. 11 / 25 Main Algorithm Families Two high-level families of methods Value-based methods Learn values such as Q(s, a) and act by choosing high-value actions. Policy-based methods Optimize the policy directly, often with gradients. Actor-critic methods Combine both: an actor chooses actions and a critic estimates value. This actor-critic vocabulary is especially useful later for PPO and RLHF. 12 / 25 Main Algorithm Families Q-learning in one slide ▶ Q-learning is an off-policy temporal-difference method. ▶ It updates action values from sampled transitions. i h ′ Q(s , a ) − Q(s , a ) Q(st , at ) ← Q(st , at ) + α rt+1 + γ max t+1 t t ′ a ▶ The bracketed term is the TD error. ▶ If state and action spaces are small, a table can work. ▶ For large spaces, we need function approximation. Limitation For language generation, the action space is huge, which makes pure Q-learning awkward. 13 / 25 Main Algorithm Families Policy gradients in one slide Instead of learning action values and taking an argmax, we directly optimize a parameterized policy πθ .   J(θ) = Eτ ∼πθ G (τ ) " # X ∇θ J(θ) ≈ E ∇θ log πθ (at | st ) Gt t ▶ This is the core REINFORCE idea. ▶ Increase probability of actions that led to high return. ▶ Decrease probability of actions that led to poor return. 14 / 25 Main Algorithm Families Why baselines and advantages help Plain policy gradient estimates can have high variance. " # X  ∇θ J(θ) ≈ E ∇θ log πθ (at | st ) Gt − b(st ) t ▶ b(st ) is a baseline, often an estimate of the value function. ▶ The difference A(st , at ) = Q(st , at ) − V (st ) is the advantage. ▶ Advantage tells us whether an action was better or worse than expected in that state. Intuition The critic says what was expected; the actor learns from whether reality was better or worse. 15 / 25 Main Algorithm Families From tabular RL to deep RL ▶ Tabular methods store one value per state or state-action pair. ▶ Deep RL uses neural networks to approximate policies or value functions. ▶ This enables image, text, and continuous-control problems. observation neural net policy or value But function approximation introduces instability, overestimation, and sensitivity to hyperparameters. 16 / 25 Main Algorithm Families Practical headaches in RL ▶ Sample inefficiency: agents may need huge amounts of experience. ▶ Reward misspecification: the reward may not capture what we really want. ▶ Instability: gradients can be noisy; learning can collapse. ▶ Distribution shift: the agent changes the data it sees as it improves. ▶ Evaluation: average reward may hide safety or robustness failures. One famous lesson RL systems optimize the metric you give them, not the intention you had in mind. 17 / 25 Main Algorithm Families Reward design and reward hacking ▶ If the reward is flawed, the policy may exploit the loophole. ▶ This is called reward hacking or specification gaming. Examples Mitigations ▶ game agent loops to collect points forever ▶ better reward design ▶ recommender learns clickbait ▶ human feedback ▶ dialogue model over-optimizes superficial preferences ▶ offline evaluation and auditing ▶ constraints and safety checks 18 / 25 Main Algorithm Families From RL to RLHF: a preview 1 Start from a pretrained language model. 2 Do supervised fine-tuning (SFT). 3 Learn a reward model from preference comparisons. SFT model 4 Optimize the policy with an RL-style update, often PPO in the classic pipeline. reward model pretrained LM policy update You do not need the LLM details yet; the point is that the basic RL vocabulary transfers directly. 19 / 25 Main Algorithm Families Why PPO became popular in post-training ▶ PPO is a policy-gradient-style method with clipped updates. ▶ It tries to improve the policy while avoiding overly large parameter steps. ▶ In LLM post-training, this helps keep the updated model near a reasonable reference policy. Pedagogical takeaway For this class, remember the concepts rather than the exact PPO objective: actor, critic, advantage, trust region intuition, and stable improvement. 20 / 25 Main Algorithm Families Where general RL ideas map onto language modeling RL term NLP / LLM analogue state prompt, dialogue context, partial generation action token, action choice, tool call, response policy language model distribution over next steps reward preference score, task success, utility, safety metric trajectory full generated sequence or multi-turn interaction critic / value estimate of future usefulness or return exploration sampling, candidate generation, online experimentation This analogy is imperfect, but it is a useful mental bridge. 21 / 25 Limits, Ethics, and Takeaways What RL is good at - and not good at Good fit ▶ long-term objectives Hard cases ▶ badly specified rewards ▶ sequential choices ▶ sparse or unsafe exploration ▶ interactive systems ▶ weak simulators ▶ delayed and partial feedback ▶ very expensive evaluation 22 / 25 Limits, Ethics, and Takeaways A compact taxonomy to remember RL value-based actor-critic model-free policy-based model-based offline RL Do not memorize every branch. Memorize the organizing questions: ▶ Are we learning values, policies, or both? ▶ Are we using a model of the environment? ▶ Are we learning online or from a fixed dataset? 23 / 25 Limits, Ethics, and Takeaways Summary ▶ RL studies how agents learn to act to maximize long-term reward. ▶ The core objects are states, actions, rewards, returns, policies, and value functions. ▶ Major difficulties are exploration, credit assignment, sparse rewards, and reward misspecification. ▶ Major families are value-based, policy-based, and actor-critic methods. ▶ These ideas reappear in NLP through bandits, sequence optimization, RLHF, and preference-based post-training. One sentence to remember RL is what you use when the quality of an action depends on what happens later. 24 / 25 Limits, Ethics, and Takeaways References Richard S. Sutton and Andrew G. Barto. Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction. Second edition. Csaba Szepesvari. Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning. David Silver. Reinforcement Learning Course (video lectures). John Schulman et al. Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms. Long Ouyang et al. Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback. 25 / 25

title: Post-training for LLMs
section: Part IV · Attention, Transformers, and Large Language Models
text: Post-training for LLMs CS115B – Spring 2026 James Pustejovsky April 10, 2026 1 / 60 Today’s place in the pipeline Pretraining: next-token prediction on large raw corpora. Post-training: modify the pretrained policy to be more helpful, safe, steerable, and often better at reasoning. Three big phases in today’s lecture: 1 2 3 supervised instruction tuning (SFT), preference alignment (RM, RLHF, DPO-family), test-time compute and reranking. Main question: how do we change the objective from “predict web text” to “behave the way we want”? 2 / 60 Why post-training exists Base model mismatch Pretraining optimizes max θ X log πθ (xt | x<t ), t but users want instruction following, truthfulness, harmlessness, format control, and often multi-step reasoning. A base model completes text; it does not automatically obey instructions. Prompting helps, but only up to the capabilities latent in the pretrained model. Post-training reshapes the model distribution πθ (y | x ) over responses y given prompt x . 3 / 60 Instruction tuning From prompt completion to instruction following Base LM view Instruction-tuned view Continue text plausibly Map instruction → useful response Sensitive to prompt wording Prefer assistant-style completions May imitate bad internet behavior Better zero-shot generalization across tasks x = “Translate to French: the small dog” ⇝ y = “le petit chien” instead of merely continuing the prompt with another English sentence. 4 / 60 Instruction tuning Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): data format Each training example is a prompt-response pair (xi , yi ) where xi may include system instructions, user turns, tool context, demonstrations, or formatting constraints. Typical chat serialization: <bos><system>...<user> xi <assistant> yi The architecture is unchanged. The objective is still token-level cross-entropy. The supervision is now task-conditioned: there is a preferred answer. 5 / 60 Instruction tuning SFT objective For dataset DSFT = {(xi , yi )}N i=1 , maximize LSFT (θ) = N X i=1 log πθ (yi | xi ) = |yi | N X X log πθ (yi,t | xi , yi,<t ). i=1 t=1 Equivalent minimization form: JSFT (θ) = −E(x ,y )∼DSFT [log πθ (y | x )]. Interpretation We are not changing the model family; we are changing the training distribution and target continuations. 6 / 60 Instruction tuning Masking: train on assistant tokens only In chat SFT we often ignore loss on prompt tokens and optimize only the assistant span: J(θ) = − T X mt log πθ (zt | z<t ), mt ∈ {0, 1} t=1 where mt = 1 only for assistant tokens. Prevents the model from wasting capacity modeling fixed prompt wrappers. Lets us train on multi-turn transcripts without penalizing the model for user text. Common implementation: labels for masked tokens are set to −100 in PyTorch cross-entropy. 7 / 60 Instruction tuning What makes instruction data valuable? 1 Coverage: many tasks, domains, languages, and styles. 2 Diversity: multiple phrasings for the same task. 3 Quality: good outputs, not just plausible outputs. 4 Formatting: explicit schemas, refusal style, citation style, verbosity control. Rule of thumb Post-training quality is often bottlenecked more by data curation than by optimizer sophistication. 8 / 60 Instruction tuning Where instruction data comes from Human-written prompts and answers Existing supervised NLP datasets turned into instruction format Synthetic data from stronger LLMs Distillation from expert systems / tools Safety-specific data: benign requests, harmful requests, jailbreak attempts, refusal exemplars Key tension: cheap synthetic scale vs. high-fidelity human supervision 9 / 60 Instruction tuning Instruction tuning as conditional distribution shift Before SFT, the model approximates pweb (y | x ). After SFT, it is pushed toward passistant (y | x ), where passistant emphasizes direct answers, formatting, politeness, hedging when uncertain, and task completion. SFT does behavior shaping. It is still imitation learning. It cannot easily optimize subtle human preferences unless those are already encoded in demonstrations. 10 / 60 Instruction tuning What SFT does not solve well Fine-grained tradeoffs such as helpfulness vs. harmlessness Ranking two plausible responses when both look acceptable Long-horizon exploration or search behavior Robust refusal under adversarial prompting Reward hacking induced by benchmark-specific exemplars Motivation for preference alignment We often care more about relative preference between outputs than exact token matching. 11 / 60 Preference alignment Preference data Instead of a single gold answer, collect comparisons: (x , y + , y − ) where for prompt x , annotators prefer y + over y − . Easier to elicit than perfect demonstrations Better aligned with product questions: “which answer is better?” Supports training a reward model or direct preference objective 12 / 60 Preference alignment Bradley–Terry preference model Suppose a latent reward model rϕ (x , y ) scores responses. Then Pϕ (y + ≻ y − | x ) =  exp(rϕ (x , y + )) = σ rϕ (x , y + ) − rϕ (x , y − ) . exp(rϕ (x , y + )) + exp(rϕ (x , y − )) Only differences in reward matter. Rewards are identifiable only up to an additive constant. This is the standard pairwise-comparison model behind many alignment methods. 13 / 60 Preference alignment Reward model training loss Given preference triples (x , y + , y − ), maximize the log-likelihood: LRM (ϕ) = X log σ rϕ (x , y + ) − rϕ (x , y − ) .  (x ,y + ,y − ) Equivalent minimization: JRM (ϕ) = −E log σ rϕ (x , y + ) − rϕ (x , y − ) .   Interpretation The reward model learns a scalar utility proxy from comparisons, not from absolute scores. 14 / 60 Preference alignment Where reward models come from architecturally Common setup: Start from an SFT model or pretrained LM encoder-decoder / decoder-only stack. Feed the entire prompt-response sequence. Take final hidden state h(x , y ), attach a scalar head: rϕ (x , y ) = w ⊤ h(x , y ) + b. Train with the pairwise logistic loss from the previous slide. Important The reward model is not deployed directly to users; it is used to shape the policy. 15 / 60 Preference alignment RLHF pipeline at a glance Pretrained model → SFT model → Preference data → Reward model → RL optimization At RL time: 1 Sample response y ∼ πθ (· | x ) 2 Score it with rϕ (x , y ) 3 Update policy to increase expected reward 4 Regularize toward a reference policy πref 16 / 60 Preference alignment KL-regularized RLHF objective A standard objective is   J(θ) = Ex ∼D, y ∼πθ (·|x ) rϕ (x , y ) − βKL(πθ (· | x ) ∥ πref (· | x )) . Equivalent token-level approximation for a sampled response: r̂ (x , y ) = rϕ (x , y ) − β X t log πθ (yt | x , y<t ) . πref (yt | x , y<t ) Reward term says “be preferred”. KL term says “do not drift too far from the reference model”. 17 / 60 Preference alignment Why the KL penalty matters Without KL regularization, the policy can exploit imperfections in the reward model: max Ey ∼πθ [rϕ (x , y )] θ may produce bizarre, high-reward but low-quality responses. Role of the reference policy πref anchors the policy to the SFT model, preserving fluency and basic task competence while still allowing improvement. Too small β: reward hacking, mode collapse Too large β: almost no behavioral change 18 / 60 Preference alignment Policy gradient view For episodic text generation, ∇θ J(θ) = Ey ∼πθ   r̂ (x , y ) − b(x ) ∇θ log πθ (y | x )  where b(x ) is a baseline to reduce variance. Tokenized form: X log πθ (y | x ) = log πθ (yt | x , y<t ). t Same REINFORCE idea as in classical RL High variance motivates PPO-style stabilization 19 / 60 Preference alignment PPO surrogate objective Given old policy πθold , define token- or sequence-level ratio ρ(θ) = πθ (y | x ) . πθold (y | x ) PPO maximizes the clipped surrogate: LPPO (θ) = E min ρ(θ)A, clip(ρ(θ), 1 − ϵ, 1 + ϵ)A .   A is an advantage estimate from the reward model plus KL shaping. Clipping prevents unstable policy jumps. In language models, PPO is usually run on top of an SFT initialization. 20 / 60 Preference alignment RLHF strengths and weaknesses Strengths Weaknesses Can optimize arbitrary scalar rewards Complex and expensive Supports online data collection Reward model misspecification Handles multi-objective reward design Credit assignment is noisy Sensitive to KL coefficient, rollout mix, truncation This motivated direct preference optimization methods that avoid an explicit RL loop. 21 / 60 Direct preference optimization DPO: core idea Instead of preferences → reward model → RL policy update, DPO collapses the pipeline into one supervised-like objective on preference pairs. Idea If the optimal RLHF policy has a closed-form relation to rewards and a reference model, then we can optimize that relation directly. 22 / 60 Direct preference optimization From KL-constrained RL to optimal policy For a fixed prompt x , consider max Ey ∼π [r (x , y )] − βKL(π(· | x )∥πref (· | x )). π(·|x ) The optimizer is the Boltzmann policy  π ∗ (y | x ) ∝ πref (y | x ) exp Thus r (x , y ) = β log 1 r (x , y ) . β  π ∗ (y | x ) + C (x ) πref (y | x ) for some prompt-dependent constant C (x ). 23 / 60 Direct preference optimization DPO loss Substitute the implied reward difference into the Bradley–Terry model: ! P(y + ≻y − πθ (y + | x ) πθ (y − | x ) | x ) = σ β log − β log . πref (y + | x ) πref (y − | x ) Then minimize " JDPO (θ) = −E(x ,y + ,y − ) πθ (y − | x ) πθ (y + | x ) − β log log σ β log πref (y + | x ) πref (y − | x ) !# . 24 / 60 Direct preference optimization How to read the DPO equation Define sequence log-probability gap ∆θ = log πθ (y + | x ) − log πθ (y − | x ). Define reference gap ∆ref = log πref (y + | x ) − log πref (y − | x ). Then DPO prefers ∆θ > ∆ref . Increase probability of chosen responses Decrease probability of rejected responses But only relative to what the reference already knows 25 / 60 Direct preference optimization Gradient intuition for DPO For one pair, ∇θ J ∝ − 1 − σ(z) β ∇θ log πθ (y + | x ) − ∇θ log πθ (y − | x )  where   + −   |x ) πθ (y |x ) z = β log ππrefθ (y (y + |x ) − log πref (y − |x ) . Takeaway The update looks like a contrastive supervised signal over full responses. 26 / 60 Direct preference optimization DPO versus RLHF Intermediate reward model Online rollouts needed Optimization style Implementation complexity Can optimize arbitrary scalar reward RLHF DPO yes usually yes RL / PPO high stronger no no supervised-like moderate weaker DPO is often easier to train and reproduce, but it still inherits the quality limits of the preference data. 27 / 60 Direct preference optimization Beyond DPO: a family of preference objectives The field now includes many close relatives: IPO: changes the classification geometry / implicit preference margin ORPO: combines odds-ratio preference loss with SFT in one stage KTO: uses Kahneman-Tversky style gains/losses with binary desirability labels SimPO, cDPO, robust DPO: address overconfidence, label noise, or calibration Pedagogical point Most of these are variants of contrastive policy shaping against a reference distribution. 28 / 60 Reasoning-focused and group-based optimization Outcome rewards versus process rewards For a reasoning trace z = (z1 , . . . , zT ) and final answer a: Routcome (x , z, a) = 1[a = a⋆ ] rewards only correctness. A process reward model instead scores intermediate steps: Rprocess (x , z) = T X rt (x , z≤t ). t=1 Outcome rewards are cheap but sparse. Process rewards are denser but require more annotation or synthetic supervision. 29 / 60 Reasoning-focused and group-based optimization Group-relative policy optimization (GRPO): intuition A prompt x generates K sampled completions y (1) , . . . , y (K ) ∼ πθ (· | x ). Each completion gets score R (k) . Use a relative advantage inside the group: A(k) = R (k) − µR σR + ϵ or A(k) = R (k) − 1 X (j) R . K j Idea Improve the samples that were better than the prompt-local average, suppress the worse ones. 30 / 60 Reasoning-focused and group-based optimization A GRPO-style objective A simplified clipped objective mirrors PPO but with group-relative advantage: X  1 K LGRPO (θ) = E min ρk (θ)A(k) , clip(ρk (θ), 1 − ϵ, 1 + ϵ)A(k) − βKL(πθ ∥πref ). K k=1 " # ρk (θ) = πθ (y (k) | x ) . πθold (y (k) | x ) This avoids a separately trained scalar value model in some implementations. 31 / 60 Constitutional and AI-feedback methods RLAIF and Constitutional AI Human preferences are expensive. Alternative: 1 Write a constitution or rubric 2 Use a stronger model to critique / revise outputs 3 Train on AI-generated preferences or revised targets policy → critique → revision → new training signal This can scale safety and style alignment beyond pure human labeling. 32 / 60 Constitutional and AI-feedback methods Constitutional training as self-revision A simplified two-stage recipe: y0 ∼ πθ (· | x ) c = Critique(x , y0 ; C) y1 = Revise(x , y0 , c; C) where C is a set of principles. Then train on revised outputs y1 or use pairwise preferences y1 ≻ y0 . Key idea Turn normative principles into synthetic supervision. 33 / 60 Constitutional and AI-feedback methods Alignment is multi-objective optimization We rarely optimize one scalar notion of “good”. A useful conceptual objective is R(x , y ) = λh Rhelp (x , y ) + λs Rsafe (x , y ) + λt Rtruth (x , y ) + λf Rformat (x , y ). The λ’s change by application. Product behavior depends heavily on how these objectives are weighted. Safety failures often arise from misspecified tradeoffs, not only from model capability. 34 / 60 Constitutional and AI-feedback methods Failure modes in alignment Reward hacking: exploit reward model quirks Over-refusal: safe but unhelpful Sycophancy: agree with the user rather than with evidence Verbosity bias: longer answers may look better to raters Distribution shift: preference data does not cover deployment prompts One deep lesson “Aligned to the data pipeline” is not the same as “aligned to the real world”. 35 / 60 Test-time compute Training-time compute versus test-time compute Two ways to improve quality: 1 make the model better before inference, 2 spend more compute during inference. Formalize a budgeted decision problem: max inference policy E[utility] s.t. E[tokens + tool calls + latency] ≤ B. Post-training increasingly teaches models how to use extra inference budget well. 36 / 60 Test-time compute Chain-of-thought as latent computation A reasoning trace z can be treated as latent or explicit computation: p(a | x ) = X z p(a, z | x ) = X p(z | x )p(a | x , z). z Approximations: sample one z (single chain) sample many z’s and marginalize approximately search over z with a verifier 37 / 60 Test-time compute Self-consistency Sample K chains of thought: z (1) , . . . , z (K ) ∼ pθ (z | x ), a(k) ∼ pθ (a | x , z (k) ). Then aggregate, often by majority vote: â = arg max a K X 1[a(k) = a]. k=1 Why it helps If multiple reasoning paths independently converge to the same answer, aggregation reduces variance. 38 / 60 Test-time compute Best-of-N sampling and reranking Generate N candidates: y (1) , . . . , y (N) ∼ πθ (· | x ). Choose ŷ = arg max s(x , y (k) ), k≤N where s may come from: a reward model, a verifier, a classifier for correctness / safety / style, a committee or ensemble. This is often the simplest effective form of test-time compute. 39 / 60 Test-time compute Verifier-guided decoding Suppose a verifier estimates vψ (x , y ) ≈ P(response is correct | x , y ). Then we can decode with combined score s(x , y ) = α log πθ (y | x ) + (1 − α) log vψ (x , y ). Language model ensures fluency and plausibility. Verifier pushes toward correctness. Common in math and code settings with executable checks. 40 / 60 Test-time compute Search over reasoning trajectories Instead of sampling full solutions independently, do incremental search over partial traces z≤t . A generic objective:   ẑ = arg max log pθ (z | x ) + λVψ (x , z) z∈T (x ) where T (x ) is the search tree and Vψ estimates downstream value. Methods: beam search over reasoning traces tree search / MCTS-like expansions branch-and-bound with tool feedback 41 / 60 Test-time compute Test-time compute changes the training target If deployment uses reranking or search, the model need not place all probability mass on the single best trajectory. Instead, a useful training target may be: produce a candidate set containing a high-quality solution. Implication Post-training can optimize for sample quality under selection, not only one-shot greedy quality. 42 / 60 Practical post-training engineering Parameter-efficient post-training Often we do not update all parameters. With LoRA, a weight matrix update is W ′ = W + ∆W , ∆W = BA, where A ∈ Rr ×din , B ∈ Rdout ×r , and r ≪ d. Train only A, B, freeze W Memory and optimizer state scale with r , not with full model size Used for SFT and often for preference tuning as well 43 / 60 Practical post-training engineering Why LoRA works surprisingly well A full update ∆W is high-dimensional, but task adaptation may lie in a low-rank subspace. Parameter count comparison: dout din vs. | {z } full finetune r (dout + din ) . | {z LoRA } For r ≪ min(din , dout ), this is a large reduction. 44 / 60 Practical post-training engineering Quantized post-training (QLoRA intuition) Store pretrained weights in low precision, e.g. 4-bit, while training LoRA adapters in higher precision. Conceptually: Wfp16 ≈ dequant(W4bit ) during forward pass, while only adapter weights receive gradients. Makes SFT / DPO feasible on much smaller hardware Does not remove the need for high-quality data Often shifts the bottleneck from memory to data and experimentation time 45 / 60 Practical post-training engineering Preference data pipeline in practice 1 Collect prompts from real or synthetic traffic 2 Sample multiple responses from current policy 3 Filter for toxicity / formatting / privacy 4 Ask raters or judges to compare responses 5 Train RM or DPO-style objective 6 Evaluate, red-team, refresh data Online loop Deployment changes the prompt distribution, so post-training is not a one-shot process. 46 / 60 Practical post-training engineering Evaluation after post-training There is no single metric. Common buckets: task quality / win rate instruction following safety and jailbreak resistance factuality / hallucination rate reasoning accuracy on held-out tasks style adherence and latency good post-training ̸= high reward-model score only 47 / 60 Practical post-training engineering Offline metrics can mislead Suppose s(x , y ) is the metric used in development. Then optimizing max E[s(x , y )], θ y ∼ πθ (· | x ) may overfit quirks of s, especially if s is itself model-based. Benchmark saturation evaluator overfitting contamination poor correlation with user satisfaction 48 / 60 Practical post-training engineering Safety post-training and refusal style Safety alignment is not just binary refusal. A more realistic target is a policy that maps ( x 7→ useful answer brief safe refusal / redirect if request is allowed if request is unsafe Need both benign and adversarial data Need calibrated refusal boundaries Need style consistency under pressure / jailbreaking 49 / 60 Practical post-training engineering Serving tradeoffs: alignment tax and product constraints Post-training can change: latency, verbosity, tool-use frequency, refusal rate, answer calibration. Useful deployment objective: Utility = quality − λ1 latency − λ2 unsafe rate − λ3 user frustration. The best research model is not automatically the best product model. 50 / 60 Worked examples Worked example: SFT loss on one chat example Suppose prompt x is fixed and target response tokens are y1 , y2 , y3 . Then log πθ (y | x ) = log πθ (y1 | x ) + log πθ (y2 | x , y1 ) + log πθ (y3 | x , y1:2 ). If the model probabilities assigned are 0.7, 0.5, 0.2, then − log πθ (y | x ) = − log(0.7) − log(0.5) − log(0.2). Low probability on any one token raises the sequence loss sharply. 51 / 60 Worked examples Worked example: reward model preference probability S

title: Scaling
sub: Condensed slides
section: Part IV · Attention, Transformers, and Large Language Models
text: Scaling Laws for Language Models From Power Laws to Compute-Optimal Training CS115B – Spring 2026 James Pustejovsky April 14, 2026 CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 1 / 20 Today’s Question If someone gave you $100 million to train the best possible language model, how would you spend it? This is not hypothetical – companies face exactly this decision. The answer changed dramatically between 2020 and 2022, and it’s still evolving. Today: The science behind that decision. Next time: How modern architectures (Mixture of Experts) put that science into practice. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 2 / 20 Three Knobs to Turn Every training run is defined by three quantities: Model Size N Number of parameters trade-off Dataset Size D Number of training tokens Compute Budget C Total FLOPs C ≈ 6ND The 6ND rule: forward pass ≈ 2N FLOPs/token, backward ≈ 4N, times D tokens. The central question: Given a fixed budget C , how do you split between a bigger model (N) and more data (D)? CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 3 / 20 Why Cross-Entropy Loss? Scaling laws predict cross-entropy loss, not task accuracy. Why? D 1 X L=− log Pθ (xi | x<i ) D i=1 Smooth and continuous – you can fit curves to it Well-defined across model sizes and architectures Connected to perplexity: PPL = e L Lower bound: Entropy of natural text ≈ 1.69 nats – no model can do better Task accuracy is noisy, task-dependent, and can show discontinuities. Loss is the clean signal that makes scaling laws possible. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 4 / 20 What Is a Power Law? log(loss) A power law: y = a · x b . In log-log space, this is a straight line. 1 0 −1 −2 −3 slope = b 0 1 2 3 log(scale) 4 5 NLP has known about power laws for a century: Zipf’s law (word frequencies), Heaps’ law (vocabulary growth). The discovery: LM loss also follows power laws in N, D, and C – over seven orders of magnitude. This means you can predict a 100B model’s loss from experiments at 100M. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 5 / 20 Kaplan et al. (2020): The First Scaling Laws Paper Kaplan, McCandlish, Henighan, Brown, Chess, Child, Gray, Radford, Wu, Amodei. Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models. OpenAI, January 2020. Four key findings: 1 Loss follows power laws in N, D, and C – remarkably predictable 2 Architecture details don’t matter much: Width vs. depth, number of heads, FFN ratio – all secondary to total parameter count 3 Larger models are more sample-efficient: A bigger model reaches the same loss with fewer tokens 4 Scale N faster than D: For 10× more compute, make the model 5.5× bigger but use only 1.8× more data Finding 4 directly shaped GPT-3’s design. But it would turn out to be wrong. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 6 / 20 The Kaplan Recipe Kaplan recommended: Nopt ∝ C 0.73 , Dopt ∝ C 0.27 . In plain English: When you get more compute, mostly make the model bigger. Don’t worry too much about more data. The industry followed this advice: Model Parameters Training Tokens GPT-3 (OpenAI, 2020) 175B 300B Gopher (DeepMind, 2021) 280B 300B Megatron-Turing NLG (2022) 530B 270B Notice: nearly the same amount of data every time, despite 3× bigger models. Question: Should a 530B model really see the same data as a 175B model? CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 7 / 20 What Kaplan Got Right (and Wrong) Right – and still standing: Loss follows power laws (confirmed by everyone since) Architecture details matter less than scale Larger models are more sample-efficient Wrong – due to a methodological issue: All models were trained with the same long cosine LR schedule When estimating loss for shorter training runs, they read off intermediate values At those intermediate points, the learning rate hadn’t decayed yet – loss was artificially high This made short training look worse than it actually is Bias: Favor bigger models trained for fewer steps If you match the LR schedule to each training horizon, the picture changes dramatically. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 8 / 20 Hoffmann et al. (2022): The Chinchilla Correction Paper Hoffmann, Borgeaud, Mensch, et al. Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models. DeepMind, March 2022. Central claim: Existing LLMs are significantly undertrained. For the same compute, a smaller model on more data wins. Evidence: Trained 400+ models (70M to 16B params, 5B to 500B tokens) Three independent analysis methods, all converging on the same answer Validated by training Chinchilla: 70B params, 1.4T tokens Chinchilla used the same compute as Gopher (280B, 300B tokens) but outperformed it on nearly every benchmark. 4× smaller, 4× more data. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 9 / 20 Three Approaches, One Answer Hoffmann et al. used three independent methods to find the optimal (N, D) for a given C : a where Nopt ∝ C a b where Dopt ∝ C b 1. Training curve envelope 0.50 0.50 2. IsoFLOP profiles 0.49 0.51 3. Parametric loss function 0.46 0.54 Kaplan et al. (2020) 0.73 0.27 Method All three say the same thing: scale N and D equally. a ≈ b ≈ 0.5. For 10× more compute: Kaplan says 5.5× model / 1.8× data. Chinchilla says ∼ 3.2× each. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 10 / 20 The Parametric Loss Function Hoffmann’s third approach gives us an intuitive decomposition: L̂(N, D) = E |{z} + entropy of natural text A Nα |{z} model isn’t big enough + B Dβ |{z} haven’t seen enough data Three sources of loss: 1 E ≈ 1.69: The floor. Even a perfect model can’t predict language perfectly. 2 A/N α : The model capacity penalty. Shrinks as you add parameters. 3 B/D β : The data penalty. Shrinks as you train on more tokens. To minimize L̂ under the constraint C = 6ND, you need to balance the two penalty terms. If you spend all your compute on a huge model with little data, B/D β dominates. If you train a tiny model on mountains of data, A/N α dominates. The optimum: balance them. This is why the exponents come out near 0.5. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 11 / 20 The 20× Rule From Hoffmann’s analysis, a simple rule of thumb: Chinchilla Rule of Thumb A compute-optimal model should train on roughly 20 tokens per parameter. Parameters Optimal Tokens Ratio 1B 20B 20× 10B 205B ∼20× 70B 1.5T ∼21× 175B 3.7T ∼21× GPT-3 (175B) trained on 300B tokens – a ratio of 1.7×. By this analysis, it needed 12× more data. It was severely undertrained. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 12 / 20 Chinchilla vs. Gopher: The Experiment Gopher Chinchilla Parameters 280B 70B Training tokens 300B 1.4T Training FLOPs 5.76 × 1023 5.76 × 1023 Same compute budget. 4× fewer parameters, ∼5× more data. Result: Chinchilla outperforms Gopher on: Every subset of The Pile (language modeling) MMLU: 67.6% vs. 60.0% (knowledge) RACE-h: 82.3% vs. 71.6% (reading comprehension) HellaSwag, Winogrande, BoolQ, LAMBADA . . . And being 4× smaller, Chinchilla is ∼4× cheaper to serve at inference. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 13 / 20 Did the Industry Listen? Model Params Tokens Tokens/Params Pre-Chinchilla (Kaplan recipe) GPT-3 (2020) 175B 300B 1.7× Gopher (2021) 280B 300B 1.1× Chinchilla (2022) 70B 1.4T 20× Llama 1 (2023) 65B 1.4T 22× Chinchilla-era Post-Chinchilla (over-training) Llama 2 (2023) 70B 2.0T 29× Llama 3 (2024) 70B 15T 214× Mistral 7B (2023) 7B >1T >140× Notice: recent models train on far more than 20× their parameters. Why? CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 14 / 20 Over-Training: When Inference Cost Matters More Chinchilla-optimal minimizes loss per training FLOP. But in production, inference cost dominates. Training is paid once; inference is paid every query. The inference-aware trade-off: A 70B model costs ∼10× more per query than a 7B model If you serve billions of queries, inference ≫ training cost Solution: Train a smaller model for much longer than Chinchilla-optimal Example: Llama 3 8B trained on 15T tokens (1875× params). Chinchilla says an 8B model needs ∼160B tokens. Llama 3 uses ∼94× more than that. The extra training compute is a one-time cost that buys a smaller, cheaper model forever. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 15 / 20 The Data Wall If compute-optimal training needs ∼20× tokens per parameter: Model Size Optimal Tokens Challenge 1B 20B Easy 70B 1.4T Achievable 1T 20T ≈ total high-quality web text 10T 200T Exceeds all available text Rough estimates of available high-quality text: ∼10–20T tokens total (web, books, code, academic papers combined). Implication: We may run out of data before we run out of compute. This is one of the pressures driving interest in synthetic data, multi-modal training, and architectures that are more data-efficient. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 16 / 20 A Different Kind of Scaling Scaling laws tell us about making models bigger. But there are other ways to scale: Inference-time compute: Chain-of-thought, best-of-N sampling, reasoning models (o1, R1) – spend more compute per question Data quality: A curated token may be worth 5–10× a random web token. Can we define “effective tokens”? Sparse activation: Have many parameters, but only use a subset per token. This is Mixture of Experts – our next lecture. MoE is in some sense the natural response to the scaling dilemma: if more parameters help but more compute hurts, decouple the two. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 17 / 20 Timeline Kaplan et al. Scale N fast Nopt ∝ C 0.73 Gopher: 280B 300B tokens 2020 2021 GPT-3: 175B 300B tokens Llama 1/2 1.4–2T tokens 2022–23 Chinchilla: 70B 1.4T tokens Nopt ∝ C 0.5 2024–25 Llama 3: 70B 15T tokens The arc: Scale parameters (Kaplan) → Scale data equally (Chinchilla) → Over-train small models for inference (Llama 3) → Use sparse models to get both (MoE – next time). CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 18 / 20 Key Takeaways 1 Loss follows power laws in N, D, and C – predictable over seven orders of magnitude. 2 Kaplan (2020) found the laws and recommended scaling N faster than D. A methodological issue (fixed LR schedule) led to this bias. 3 Chinchilla (2022) corrected the allocation: scale N and D equally (∼ C 0.5 each). Most 2020–22 LLMs were undertrained. 4 The 20× rule: Train on ∼20 tokens per parameter for compute-optimality. 5 In practice, inference cost pushes toward smaller models trained much longer (over-training). 6 The data wall looms: at trillion-parameter scale, we may not have enough text. Next Time Mixture of Experts: architectures that decouple capacity from cost. Read: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super Technical Report (§2.1). CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 19 / 20 References Kaplan, J., McCandlish, S., Henighan, T., Brown, T.B., et al. (2020). Scaling laws for neural language models. arXiv:2001.08361. Hoffmann, J., Borgeaud, S., Mensch, A., Buchatskaya, E., et al. (2022). Training compute-optimal large language models. arXiv:2203.15556. Brown, T.B., et al. (2020). Language models are few-shot learners. NeurIPS 2020. Rae, J., et al. (2021). Scaling language models: Methods, analysis & insights from training Gopher. arXiv:2112.11446. Touvron, H., et al. (2023). Llama: Open and efficient foundation language models. arXiv:2302.13971. Touvron, H., et al. (2023). Llama 2: Open foundation and fine-tuned chat models. arXiv:2307.09288. Sutton, R. (2019). The bitter lesson. Blog post. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 14, 2026 20 / 20
