text: Scaling Laws for Language Models From Power Laws to Compute-Optimal Training CS115B – Spring 2026 James Pustejovsky April 13, 2026 CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 1 / 51 Roadmap (90 Minutes) ∼20 min Part I – Foundations: Why Scale Matters The empirical surprise: performance improves predictably with scale Measuring scale: parameters (N), data (D), compute (C ) Cross-entropy loss as the universal yardstick ∼25 min Part II – Kaplan et al. (2020): The First Scaling Laws Power-law relationships across seven orders of magnitude Optimal compute allocation and early stopping ∼25 min Part III – Hoffmann et al. (2022): Chinchilla Three approaches to finding the optimal frontier “Scale parameters and data equally” Chinchilla vs. Gopher: the empirical validation ∼20 min Part IV – Beyond Chinchilla: Open Questions Inference-time compute, over-training, and data quality Do scaling laws still hold? What breaks? CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 2 / 51 The Empirical Observation The Bitter Lesson (Sutton, 2019) General methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective. The history of deep learning in NLP: 2013 – Word2Vec: 300-dim vectors, ∼1M vocabulary 2018 – BERT-Large: 340M parameters 2019 – GPT-2: 1.5B parameters 2020 – GPT-3: 175B parameters 2022 – PaLM: 540B parameters 2023 – Llama 2: 7B–70B parameters 2024–25 – Llama 3, Gemini, Claude: trillions of tokens Key question: Is this growth principled, or are we just throwing compute at the wall? CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 3 / 51 Three Axes of Scale Every training run is defined by three quantities: Model Size N Number of parameters trade-off Dataset Size D Number of training tokens Compute Budget C Total FLOPs C ≈ 6ND (Kaplan et al., 2020) Given a fixed compute budget C , how should we allocate between N and D? This is the central question of scaling law research. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 4 / 51 Computing FLOPs For a standard Transformer with N parameters, trained on D tokens: Forward pass per token ≈ 2N multiply-accumulate operations. Backward pass ≈ 2× forward pass. The 6ND Approximation C ≈ 6N D (total training FLOPs) Breakdown for a single layer (forward only): Attention QKV projections: 2 × 3 × T × dmodel × dmodel Attention logits: 2 × T 2 × dmodel FFN (two linear layers): 2 × T × (dmodel × dff + dff × dmodel ) With dff = 4 dmodel and L layers: forward FLOPs ≈ 2N × T (embedding terms small for large N). CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 5 / 51 Cross-Entropy Loss as the Yardstick Why cross-entropy loss? Smooth, continuous, differentiable – ideal for curve fitting Directly connected to perplexity: PPL = e L Well-defined across model sizes and architectures Correlated with downstream task performance (generally) The loss function: D L=− 1 X log Pθ (xi | x<i ) D i=1 Lower bound: The entropy of natural text ≈ 1.69 nats (Hoffmann et al., 2022). Important: Scaling laws describe how L varies with N, D, and C – not downstream task accuracy directly. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 6 / 51 Perplexity vs. Cross-Entropy Recall the relationship: 1 P Perplexity = e L = e − D Cross-Entropy L Perplexity 4.0 3.0 2.5 2.0 1.69 54.6 20.1 12.2 7.4 5.4 i log Pθ (xi |x<i ) Interpretation Random-ish predictions Small LM territory Decent language model Strong LM (GPT-2 level) Entropy of English (floor) Scaling laws are typically plotted in log-log space: if L ∝ N −α , then log L vs. log N is a straight line with slope −α. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 7 / 51 What Is a Power Law? A power law is a relationship of the form: y = a · xb log y In log-log space: log y = log a + b · log x (a straight line!). 1 0 −1 −2 −3 slope = b 0 1 2 3 4 5 log x Power laws are ubiquitous in nature: city sizes, earthquake magnitudes, word frequencies (Zipf’s law!). The discovery that LM loss follows power laws was a major empirical finding. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 8 / 51 From Zipf to Scaling Laws NLP has long known about power laws: Zipf’s Law: The frequency of a word is inversely proportional to its rank: f (r ) ∝ r −α , α≈1 Heaps’ Law: Vocabulary size grows sub-linearly with corpus size: |V | ∝ D β , β ≈ 0.5 Scaling laws for LMs (Kaplan et al., 2020) are a new power law: L(N) ∝ N −αN , L(D) ∝ D −αD , L(C ) ∝ C −αC The surprise: These hold over seven orders of magnitude – from 768-parameter models to 1.5B-parameter models – with remarkable predictive accuracy. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 9 / 51 Kaplan et al. (2020): Overview Paper Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, Tom Henighan, Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Chess, Rewon Child, Scott Gray, Alec Radford, Jeffrey Wu, Dario Amodei. Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models. arXiv:2001.08361. Key contributions: 1 Empirical power-law relationships: L vs. N, D, and C 2 Architecture details (width, depth, #heads) matter much less than scale 3 Larger models are more sample-efficient 4 Optimal training: train very large models on relatively little data, stop early Training setup: Decoder-only Transformers on WebText2, varying N from ∼768 to ∼1.5 B. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 10 / 51 The Core Power Laws Kaplan et al. found three independent power-law relationships: Relationship Loss vs. Parameters Loss vs. Data Loss vs. Compute Formula  αN Nc L(N) =  N αD Dc L(D) =  D αC Cc L(C ) = C Exponent αN ≈ 0.076 αD ≈ 0.095 αC ≈ 0.050 Each law holds when the other factors are not bottlenecks (i.e., sufficient data when varying N, sufficient model size when varying D). CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 11 / 51 Visualizing the Power Laws In log-log space, these become straight lines: Test Loss L L vs. N L vs. C L vs. D 4.5 4.5 4.5 4 4 4 3.5 3.5 3.5 3 3 3 2.5 2.5 6 7 8 9 log N (parameters) 10 2.5 7 8 9 10 log D (tokens) 11 16 18 20 22 log C (FLOPs) Schematic illustration. The actual plots from Kaplan et al. span 7+ orders of magnitude on the x-axis, with thousands of data points falling tightly on the line. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 12 / 51 Architecture Doesn’t Matter (Much) Surprising finding: Once N is fixed, architectural details have minimal effect on L: Varied Result Width vs. depth Minimal effect across wide range of dmodel /L ratios Number of heads No significant effect (given fixed dmodel ) Feed-forward ratio dff /dmodel ∈ [1, 8]: small effect Context length Minimal effect on loss (though affects downstream tasks) Implication: The total number of parameters is what matters, not how they are arranged. Caveat: This was tested within a specific family of Transformer architectures. Different activation functions, normalization schemes, or entirely different architectures might differ. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 13 / 51 Sample Efficiency Key finding: Larger models reach the same loss with fewer data points. Test Loss L 5 Small (N1 ) Medium (N2 ) Large (N3 ) 4 3 2 0 2 4 6 Training tokens D 8 10 At the same data budget, the larger model always achieves lower loss. This suggests: if compute is limited, prefer a larger model trained for fewer steps over a smaller model trained longer. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 14 / 51 Optimal Compute Allocation (Kaplan) Given a fixed compute budget C , Kaplan et al. recommended: Kaplan Scaling Recipe Nopt ∝ C 0.73 , Dopt ∝ C 0.27 Interpretation: For a 10× increase in compute: Increase model size by ∼ 5.5× Increase training data by only ∼ 1.8× This led to a clear industry trend: GPT-3 (175B) trained on 300B tokens Gopher (280B) trained on 300B tokens Megatron-Turing NLG (530B) trained on 270B tokens Same data, bigger models. Was this the right strategy? CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 15 / 51 Kaplan’s Overfitting Analysis Kaplan et al. also derived a simple overfitting law:  L(N, D) = Nc N αN  + Dc D αD Overfitting becomes significant when D ≲ 5000 · N 0.74 . Parameters N Min. tokens D (no overfit) Ratio D/N 100M ∼2B 20× 1B ∼10B 10× 10B ∼55B 5.5× 100B ∼300B 3× Note: As models get larger, the required D/N ratio actually decreases – large models can “afford” to see proportionally less data. (But Chinchilla will challenge this April intuition.) CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws 13, 2026 16 / 51 Limitations of Kaplan et al. Several methodological choices would later prove consequential: 1 Fixed training schedule. All models used the same cosine schedule over 130B tokens – shorter runs gave intermediate losses, not final losses after proper LR decay. 2 Mostly small models. The majority of runs used models with <100M parameters. Extrapolating to 175B+ introduces risk. 3 No learning rate tuning per run. The LR schedule was not matched to the training horizon, causing systematically higher losses for shorter training runs. 4 Single dataset. All experiments used WebText2. Key consequence: Using intermediate losses from a long cosine schedule overestimates the loss of a model that would be trained with a properly matched shorter schedule. This makes short training runs look worse than they are, biasing toward larger models with less data. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 17 / 51 Summary: Kaplan et al. Takeaways 1. Loss follows power laws in N, D, C 2. Architecture details matter little But points 4 and 5 would be revised by Hoffmann et al. (2022), who showed that data should be scaled equally with parameters. 3. Larger models are more sampleefficient 4. Scale N faster than D: C 0.73 Nopt ∝ 5. Train large, stop early CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 18 / 51 Hoffmann et al. (2022): Overview Paper Jordan Hoffmann∗ , Sebastian Borgeaud∗ , Arthur Mensch∗ , Elena Buchatskaya, . . . , Laurent Sifre∗ . Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models. arXiv:2203.15556. Central claim: Current LLMs are significantly undertrained. For the same compute budget, a smaller model trained on more data outperforms a larger, data-starved model. Evidence: Trained 400+ models from 70M to 16B parameters, on 5B to 500B tokens Three independent approaches all converge on the same conclusion Validated with Chinchilla (70B params, 1.4T tokens) vs. Gopher (280B params, 300B tokens) – same compute budget CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 19 / 51 The State of LLMs in Early 2022 Model Parameters Training Tokens LaMDA (Google, 2022) 137B 168B GPT-3 (OpenAI, 2020) 175B 300B Jurassic-1 (AI21, 2021) 178B 300B Gopher (DeepMind, 2021) 280B 300B Megatron-Turing NLG (Microsoft/NVIDIA, 2022) 530B 270B Chinchilla (DeepMind, 2022) 70B 1.4T Observation: Nearly all models trained on ∼300B tokens, regardless of model size. This is Kaplan’s recipe in action. Chinchilla bucks the trend: 4× fewer parameters, 4× more data, same total compute as Gopher. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 20 / 51 The Central Question Optimization Problem Nopt (C ), Dopt (C ) = arg min L(N, D) N,D s.t. FLOPs(N, D) = C Given a budget of C FLOPs, what is the best (N, D) pair? Hoffmann et al. used three independent approaches: 1 Approach 1: Fix model sizes, vary training tokens. Extract the envelope of minimum loss per FLOP. 2 Approach 2: Fix FLOP budgets (IsoFLOP profiles), vary model size. Find the model size that minimizes loss for each budget. 3 Approach 3: Fit a parametric loss function L̂(N, D) to all runs simultaneously. All three approaches converge on the same answer. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 21 / 51 Approach 1: Training Curve Envelope Method: 1 2 Training Loss 3 Train models from 70M to 10B parameters For each model size, train for 4 different cosine schedule lengths (varying by 16×) Interpolate loss curves; for each FLOP value, find which (N, D) achieves lowest loss 5 70M 500M 4 1B 10B 3 Envelope 2 17 18 19 20 21 22 log10 FLOPs The envelope (dashed) traces the minimum achievable loss at each FLOP budget. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 22 / 51 Approach 1: Results Fitting power laws to the envelope: Approach 1 Scaling Exponents Nopt ∝ C 0.50 , Dopt ∝ C 0.50 Equal scaling! For every doubling of compute: Double the model size Double the training data Compare with Kaplan: Nopt ∝ C 0.73 , Dopt ∝ C 0.27 . Why the difference? Kaplan used intermediate losses from a fixed long cosine schedule Hoffmann matched the LR schedule to each training horizon Matching the schedule gives systematically lower final losses for shorter runs CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 23 / 51 Approach 2: IsoFLOP Profiles Training Loss Method: For each of 9 FLOP budgets (6 × 1018 to 3 × 1021 ), vary model size and find the loss-minimizing N. 6×1018 3 1×1020 3×1021 2.5 2 7.5 8 8.5 9 9.5 10 10.5 Parameters (log scale) Each U-shaped curve has a clear valley – the optimal model size for that FLOP budget. Too small → underfitting. Too large → undertrained. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 24 / 51 Approach 2: Results Approach 2 Scaling Exponents Nopt ∝ C 0.49 , Dopt ∝ C 0.51 Again: approximately equal scaling of parameters and data. Advantages of IsoFLOP profiles: Only uses final losses (not intermediate training points) Cosine schedule properly matched to each training horizon Models trained up to 16B parameters (vs. 10B in Approach 1) Projection for Gopher’s budget (5.76 × 1023 FLOPs): Optimal model: ∼63B parameters, trained on ∼1.4T tokens. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 25 / 51 Approach 3: Parametric Loss Function Model: Decompose the loss into three terms: Parametric Loss Decomposition L̂(N, D) = E |{z} + entropy of text A α N |{z} finite model approximation + B β D |{z} finite data approximation Interpretation of each term: E – irreducible loss: the entropy of natural text (≈ 1.69 nats) A/N α – how much worse a model of size N is vs. an ideal model B/D β – how much worse training on D tokens is vs. infinite data Fitted values: E = 1.69, A = 406.4, B = 410.7, α = 0.34, β = 0.28. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 26 / 51 Approach 3: Derivation of the Efficient Frontier Minimize L̂(N, D) subject to C = 6ND:  a C Nopt (C ) = G , 6 where:  G= αA βB  b C 6 b= α α+β Dopt (C ) = G  1 α+β , −1 a= β , α+β Approach 3 Scaling Exponents a= 0.28 = 0.46, 0.34 + 0.28 b= 0.34 = 0.54 0.34 + 0.28 Slightly favoring data over parameters, but still approximately equal. Note the closed-form solution – quite elegant. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 27 / 51 Comparing All Three Approaches a where Nopt ∝ C a b where Dopt ∝ C b 1. Training curve envelope 0.50 0.50 2. IsoFLOP profiles 0.49 0.51 3. Parametric loss function 0.46 0.54 Kaplan et al. (2020) 0.73 0.27 Approach Consensus: a ≈ b ≈ 0.5. Scale parameters and data equally. Kaplan’s a = 0.73 now looks like an artifact of the fixed LR schedule methodology. Practical implication: For a 10× increase in compute: Kaplan: 5.5× bigger model, 1.8× more data Chinchilla: ∼ 3.2× bigger model, ∼ 3.2× more data CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 28 / 51 Compute-Optimal Model Sizes What does the Chinchilla frontier predict? Parameters FLOPs Optimal Tokens Tokens/Params 400M 1.9 × 1019 8.0B 20× 1B 1.2 × 10 20 20.2B 20× 10B 1.2 × 10 22 205B 20× 67B 5.8 × 1023 1.5T 22× 175B 24 3.7T 21× 24 5.9T 21× 26 21.2T 21× 280B 1T 3.9 × 10 9.9 × 10 1.3 × 10 Rule of thumb: Train on roughly 20× as many tokens as you have parameters. A 175B model needs ∼3.7T tokens to be compute-optimal – over 10× more than GPT-3 used! CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 29 / 51 The LR Schedule Matters Learning Rate Critical methodological difference between Kaplan and Hoffmann: 1 stop here? Kaplan: fixed long schedule Chinchilla: matched schedule 0.5 0 0 2 4 6 8 10 Training Steps Kaplan’s approach: Train all models with a long cosine schedule; read off intermediate loss values for shorter “training horizons.” Problem: At the intermediate read-off point, the LR hasn’t decayed – the loss is artificially high. This makes short training runs look worse than they actually are. Hoffmann et al. showed that overestimating the cosine cycle by >25% leads to clear performance degradation. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 30 / 51 Chinchilla vs. Gopher: The Showdown Gopher Chinchilla Parameters 280B 70B Training tokens 300B 1.4T Training FLOPs 5.76 × 1023 5.76 × 1023 Layers 80 80 dmodel 16,384 8,192 Heads 128 64 Adam AdamW Optimizer Same compute budget. Same number of layers. Chinchilla is narrower (half dmodel ) but trains on 4.7× more tokens. If Kaplan is right, Gopher should win. If Hoffmann is right, Chinchilla should win. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 31 / 51 Chinchilla Results: Language Modeling Chinchilla outperforms Gopher on every subset of The Pile: Subset Pile-CC PubMed Abstracts StackExchange GitHub ArXiv FreeLaw Books3 Chinchilla (70B) Gopher (280B) ∆ 0.667 0.559 0.614 0.337 0.627 0.476 0.675 0.691 0.578 0.641 0.377 0.662 0.513 0.712 −0.024 −0.019 −0.027 −0.040 −0.035 −0.037 −0.037 Values are bits-per-byte (bpb); lower is better. Chinchilla wins uniformly despite having 4× fewer parameters. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 32 / 51 Chinchilla Results: Downstream Tasks Task Chinchilla Gopher GPT-3 MT-NLG 530B 80.8% 74.9% 83.7% 79.2% 70.1% 79.3% 78.9% 70.2% 60.5% 80.2% 73.0% 78.2% Reading Comprehension LAMBADA 77.4% RACE-h 82.3% 74.5% 71.6% 76.2% 46.8% 76.6% 47.9% Knowledge MMLU (5-shot) 60.0% 43.9% – Common Sense HellaSwag Winogrande BoolQ 67.6% Chinchilla (70B) outperforms all larger models on nearly every benchmark. MMLU: 67.6% exceeds human forecasters’ June 2023 prediction of 63.4%. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 33 / 51 Why Chinchilla Also Wins at Deployment Being 4× smaller has practical advantages: Gopher (280B) Chinchilla (70B) ∼560 GB ∼140 GB Inference cost 1× ∼ 0.25× Fine-tuning cost 1× ∼ 0.25× Min. GPU cluster ≥16 A100-80GB ≥4 A100-80GB GPU memory (fp16) The total cost of a model = training + inference. Training cost is paid once; inference cost is paid every query. A model that is deployed millions of times amortizes training cost quickly – the smaller inference footprint of Chinchilla is a compounding advantage. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 34 / 51 The Parametric Loss Decomposition: Deeper Dive Recall: L̂(N, D) = E + NAα + DBβ This can be derived from a classical statistical learning decomposition: L(N, D) = L(f ∗ ) + L(fN ) − L(f ∗ ) + L(f¯N,D ) − L(fN ) | {z } | {z } | {z } Bayes risk approximation error estimation error f ∗ – the Bayes-optimal predictor (entropy of text) fN – the best N-parameter transformer on infinite data f¯N,D – the transformer after one epoch on D tokens Expected scaling: Approximation error: ∼ N −1/2 for two-layer networks (Siegel & Xu, 2020) Estimation error: ∼ D −1/2 from SGD convergence rates (Robbins & Monro, 1951) Empirically: α = 0.34, β = 0.28 – both below 1/2, indicating room for improvement. CS115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) Scaling Laws April 13, 2026 35 / 51 IsoLoss Contours The fitted L̂(N, D) generates contour plots in (N, D) space: log10 Tokens 14 r 12 t ien Chinchilla ie nt fro Gopher GPT-3 MT-NLG c Effi 10 7 8 9 10 11 12 log10 Parameters The efficient frontier passes through Chinchilla. All other models sit below it (too many parameters, too few tokens). Poi

title: Mixture of Experts Models
section: Part IV · Attention, Transformers, and Large Language Models
text: Mixture of Experts and Agentic Post-Training at Scale From Sparse Routing to Multi-Environment RL CS 115B – Spring 2026 James Pustejovsky April 14, 2026 CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 1 / 39 Roadmap Part I – Mixture of Experts: The Big Idea Why sparse models? The cost-vs.-capacity dilemma How routing works (with math, explained) Load balancing and why it matters From Mixtral to LatentMoE: a brief tour Part II – Case Study: Nemotron 3 Super Architecture: Mamba + Attention + LatentMoE What makes it fast (speculative decoding, FP4 training) Part III – Teaching LLMs to Act: Agentic Post-Training From last week’s RLHF to multi-environment RL How agentic training data is made PivotRL and SWE-RL: two new ideas Open questions CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 2 / 39 The Dilemma From our scaling laws lecture, we know: More parameters → lower loss → better model. But more parameters also means: More computation per token (every parameter participates in every forward pass) More memory (all weights must be stored on GPUs) Higher cost at inference – and inference cost is paid every query Can we have a model that knows a lot but doesn’t think about everything at once? This is the idea behind Mixture of Experts: a model with many parameters, but only a fraction are used for any given input. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 3 / 39 An Analogy: The Hospital Think of a hospital with many specialists: The hospital employs 500 doctors (total capacity) But for any one patient, a triage nurse (the router) selects 2–3 relevant specialists The patient doesn’t see all 500 doctors – that would be slow and expensive The hospital’s total knowledge is vast; the cost per patient is low In a Mixture of Experts model: Doctors = expert networks (small FFNs) Patient = an input token Triage nurse = a learned routing function Total capacity = all experts combined (≫ what any one token uses) CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 4 / 39 Where MoE Lives in the Transformer In a standard Transformer layer, there are two sublayers: Standard Layer MoE Layer Self-Attention Self-Attention (unchanged) Feed-Forward Network (FFN) Router → top-k of N Experts MoE replaces only the FFN. Attention is shared – every token still attends to every other token. The sparsity is purely in the “thinking” step, not the “looking around” step. (i) (i) Each expert is itself a small FFN: Ei (x) = W2 · σ(W1 · x). CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 5 / 39 The Router: How Tokens Pick Experts Token x Router 0.6 E1 E2 E3 0.4 E4 E5 Output = 0.6 · E3 (x) + 0.4 · E4 (x) The router is a simple learned linear layer. It looks at the token and assigns a score to each expert. Only the top-k experts are activated; the rest are ignored. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 6 / 39 The Math (Explained) Step 1: Score every expert. The router is just a matrix multiply + softmax: g (x) = softmax(Wg · x) ∈ RN This gives a probability distribution over N experts. Think of it as: “How relevant is each expert to this particular token?” Step 2: Pick the top k. Select the k experts with the highest scores. Zero out the rest. Step 3: Combine. Run the token through each selected expert and mix the results: X y= ĝi (x) · Ei (x) i∈top-k where ĝi are the scores renormalized to sum to 1 over the selected experts. That’s it. The router learns which experts to consult; the experts learn what to compute. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 7 / 39 A Worked Example Imagine N = 8 experts, k = 2. Token x = the word “derivative” in a math context. Router scores: E1 E2 E3 E4 E5 E6 E7 E8 0.02 0.05 0.41 0.03 0.08 0.31 0.06 0.04 Top-2: E3 (score 0.41) and E6 (score 0.31). Renormalize: ĝ3 = 0.41/(0.41 + 0.31) = 0.57, ĝ6 = 0.43. Output: y = 0.57 · E3 (x) + 0.43 · E6 (x). Experts E1 , E2 , E4 , E5 , E7 , E8 are never computed for this token. We save 75% of the FFN computation. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 8 / 39 The Numbers Game Why does this matter at scale? Model Total Params Active / Token Ratio 70B 70B 1× Mixtral 8×7B 46.7B 12.9B 3.6× DeepSeek-V3 671B 37B 18× Nemotron 3 Super 120B 12B 10× Llama 3 70B (dense) Nemotron 3 Super has the knowledge capacity of a 120B model but the inference cost of a 12B model. The catch: You still need to store all 120B parameters in GPU memory. MoE saves compute, not storage. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 9 / 39 The Load Balancing Problem What goes wrong without intervention? The router learns to send most tokens to the same few “popular” experts. This is called expert collapse. Why it happens: Early in training, some experts get slightly better by chance. The router sends more tokens to them. They get even better (more training signal). Positive feedback loop. Why it’s bad: Most experts sit idle – wasted parameters The overloaded experts become a bottleneck on GPU utilization Effective model capacity shrinks to just a few experts Analogy: Imagine if the triage nurse always sent every patient to the same two doctors. The hospital has 500 doctors but functions like a clinic with 2. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 10 / 39 Fixing Load Balance Solution 1: Auxiliary loss (GShard, Switch Transformer): Add a penalty term to the training loss that discourages unbalanced routing: Ltotal = LLM + α · N N X fi · pi i=1 | {z } load-balancing penalty fi = fraction of tokens actually sent to expert i pi = average router probability for expert i The product fi · pi is high when an expert is both popular and frequently chosen Solution 2: Auxiliary-loss-free (DeepSeek-V3, Nemotron 3 Super): Instead of a loss term, dynamically adjust expert bias terms during training. If an expert is underused, increase its bias; if overused, decrease it. No extra hyperparameter α to tune. Modern trend is toward Solution 2 – more stable at very large scale. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 11 / 39 Shared Experts: A Safety Net Problem: Some information is useful for every token (basic syntax, common words). Forcing this through routed experts wastes routing decisions. Solution (DeepSeek-V2, Nemotron 3 Super): Add “shared” experts that run on every token, alongside the routed ones: y = E shared (x) + | {z } always active X ĝi (x) · Ei (x) i∈top-k | {z conditionally active } Think of it as: the shared expert handles the “common knowledge” that applies everywhere, freeing the routed experts to specialize in particular domains or skills. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 12 / 39 A Brief Tour: Key MoE Models Model Lab Total Experts Top-k Switch (2021) Mixtral (2023) DeepSeek-V3 (2024) Qwen3-235B (2025) Nemotron Super (2026) Google Mistral DeepSeek Alibaba NVIDIA 1.7T 47B 671B 235B 120B 2048 8 256 128 512 1 2 8 8 22 Innovation First trillion-param LM Open-source MoE Aux-loss-free routing Multi-env RL LatentMoE + Mamba Trends over five years: More experts, higher top-k (from top-1 to top-22) From auxiliary loss to auxiliary-loss-free balancing Post-training becoming as important as pre-training CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 13 / 39 Nemotron 3 Super: Three Ideas in One Model NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Super combines three architectural innovations: 1. LatentMoE 512 experts, top-22 via latent projection 2. Hybrid Mamba Efficient sequence modeling (no KV cache) 3. Multi-Token Prediction Built-in speculative decoding Result: 120B total / 12B active parameters. Matches GPT-OSS-120B accuracy with 2.2× higher throughput. Supports 1M token context. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 14 / 39 LatentMoE: The Key Insight Standard MoE: Route tokens in the full hidden dimension d. Problem: Routing traffic and expert weight reads both scale with d. This is the inference bottleneck. LatentMoE: Project tokens to a smaller dimension ℓ before routing: W↓ route + experts W↑ x ∈ Rd −−−→ z ∈ Rℓ −−−−−−−−−−→ z′ −−−→ y ∈ Rd Nemotron: d = 4096, ℓ = 1024 (4× compression). The trade: You saved 4× on routing cost. Spend it on 4× more experts: Standard MoE might use 128 experts, top-5 LatentMoE uses 512 experts, top-22 Same inference cost, but exponentially more expert combinations More combinations = more specialized responses per token. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 15 / 39 Why Mamba? The KV Cache Problem Standard attention stores a key-value pair for every past token. For a 1M-token context, this becomes enormous. Mamba (a state-space model) replaces most attention layers: Uses a fixed-size state instead of a growing KV cache Memory cost: O(1) per layer during generation (vs. O(T ) for attention) Processes sequences in linear time (vs. O(T 2 ) for attention) But Mamba alone isn’t enough. It can miss long-range dependencies that require token-to-token comparison. Nemotron’s solution: 88 layers, mostly Mamba, with a few attention “anchors” sprinkled in. The attention layers handle global routing; Mamba handles efficient local processing. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 16 / 39 Multi-Token Prediction: A Built-In Draft Model Standard LLM: Generate one token at a time (slow). Speculative decoding: Use a small “draft” model to propose several tokens, then verify them all at once with the large model. Faster, but requires two separate models. Nemotron’s MTP: Train the model itself to predict the next M tokens at each position. The prediction heads act as the built-in draft model. Innovation: Shared-weight heads. Instead of M independent heads (each predicting a fixed offset), use one head that is reused across positions. This makes it robust to its own mistakes when drafting autoregressively. Result: On average, 3.45 tokens accepted per verification step (vs. 2.70 for DeepSeek-R1). Combined with NVFP4 quantization and sparse MoE, this yields the 2.2× throughput advantage. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 17 / 39 Nemotron at a Glance Property Total / Active params Experts / Active Layers Training tokens Max context Training precision Speculative decoding Value 120B / 12B 512 / top-22 (LatentMoE) 88 (mostly Mamba + some Attention) 25 trillion 1M tokens NVFP4 (4-bit) MTP shared-weight heads Key comparisons (8K in / 64K out, B200 GPUs): vs. GPT-OSS-120B: comparable accuracy, 2.2× faster vs. Qwen3.5-122B: comparable accuracy, 7.5× faster Speed comes from all three innovations working together: sparse MoE + Mamba (less memory) + MTP (fewer decoding steps) + FP4 (less bandwidth). CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 18 / 39 Recall: The Post-Training Pipeline Last week we covered the standard pipeline: SFT Reward Model PPO / DPO / GRPO This works well for making a helpful chatbot. But what if we want the model to act in the world? Write code and fix bugs in real repositories Use terminal commands to accomplish tasks Call APIs, search the web, process results Carry out multi-step plans over dozens of turns These “agentic” capabilities require a fundamentally richer post-training recipe. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 19 / 39 Nemotron’s Post-Training Pipeline Base Model 1M context SFT 7M samples RLVR 21 envs SWE-RL RLHF Compare this to the standard 3-stage pipeline. Nemotron has four distinct RL stages after SFT: 1 RLVR – Multi-environment RL with verifiable rewards (math, code, tools, safety) 2 SWE-RL – End-to-end RL on real GitHub issues (the hardest environment) 3 RLHF – General instruction following and interaction quality Each stage targets a different aspect of capability. The order matters: broad capability first, then specialized, then polish. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 20 / 39 SFT: Two Losses, One Insight Problem: When you train on a mix of long reasoning chains and short answers, the long outputs dominate the loss. The model gets great at reasoning but forgets how to give a brief, direct answer. Nemotron’s solution – two-stage SFT: Stage 1 (token-level average): Every output token contributes equally. total loss over all output tokens L1 = total number of output tokens Long outputs get proportionally more gradient signal. Good for learning reasoning. Stage 2 (sample-level average): Every conversation contributes equally. X loss for conversation c 1 L2 = # conversations c output tokens in c A 3-token answer counts as much as a 3000-token chain-of-thought. Restores balance. Stage 1 teaches reasoning. Stage 2 teaches restraint. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 21 / 39 The Agentic Data Explosion Nemotron 3 Super’s SFT data is radically different from a standard chat dataset: Category Conversational Tool Use General Tool Use Agentic Programming Software Engineering Terminal Use Search Agent CUDA Kernels Safety Scale 279K convos 1.5M traces 28K tasks – 85K samples – 100K – What it teaches Multi-turn API calling Diverse tool formats CLI operation (Codex, etc.) Real GitHub issue resolution Bash commands in Docker Multi-hop web retrieval GPU programming Jailbreak resistance Total: 7 million samples. The agentic portion is much larger than in any prior model. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 22 / 39 How Agentic Data Is Made: A Six-Stage Pipeline Example: Conversational Tool Use data generation 1. Generate domains 2. Generate policies & tools 3. Generate scenarios 4. Simulate 16 convos per scenario 5. Judge quality 6. Keep only hard cases Step 4 is the key: three LLMs play different roles: User LLM: Simulates a customer with a specific scenario Agent LLM: Tries to help, calling tools as needed Environment LLM: Simulates tool execution and returns results Step 6 is crucial: Drop scenarios where the agent always succeeds or always fails. Keep only the informative ones – where success requires skill. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 23 / 39 From RLHF to RLVR Last week we saw RLHF: RL from Human Feedback. A neural reward model scores outputs. Nemotron primarily uses RLVR: RL from Verifiable Rewards. What’s the difference? RLHF RLVR Reward signal Neural network Program / verifier Reward noise Noisy (model errors) Exact (ground truth) Reward hacking Common Rare Domains Open-ended chat Tasks with clear answers Scalability Expensive (needs RM) Cheap per evaluation Examples: Math → check numerical answer. Code → run test cases. Tool use → check outcome. The reward is a binary “correct or not,” computed by a program. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 24 / 39 Multi-Environment RLVR Nemotron trains on 21 environments simultaneously: Math Code STEM Tool Use Terminal Inst. Follow Safety Long Ctx Puzzles Proofs ··· Why all at once? When NVIDIA tried training on one environment at a time, the model improved on that task but forgot the others (catastrophic forgetting). Simultaneous training prevents this. The algorithm is GRPO (from last week), but run asynchronously: Inference workers generate rollouts continuously Training engine updates the model when enough rollouts accumulate Updated weights are pushed to inference workers without waiting CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 25 / 39 Quick Refresher: GRPO Recall from last week – Group Relative Policy Optimization: For each prompt x: Generate G responses. Score them. Compute a relative advantage: Âi = ri − mean(r) std(r) Intuition: “How much better (or worse) is this response compared to the group average?” Update the model to increase the probability of above-average responses: L=−   1 X min ρi Âi , clip(ρi )Âi − β · KL penalty G i Nemotron specifics: 256 prompts/step × 16 responses each. Max generation: 64K tokens. Because rollouts may use slightly stale model weights (async lag), they mask the importance ratio ρi to avoid instability. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 26 / 39 Difficulty Curriculum Not all prompts are equally useful for RL training. Step 1 – Remove the easy stuff: If the SFT model already answers a prompt correctly every time, there’s nothing to learn. Filter these out. Step 2 – Sort by difficulty: Start training on easier problems, gradually introduce harder ones. This is standard curriculum learning applied to RL. Step 3 – Special handling for “low-effort” mode: For some prompts, the reward considers both correctness and brevity: rlow-effort = f (correct, |tokens|) This teaches the model to give short, efficient answers when appropriate – not every question needs a 5000-token chain of thought. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 27 / 39 PivotRL: Efficient Agentic RL The problem: End-to-end RL for agentic tasks (tool use, code editing) is very expensive. Each rollout requires launching containers, executing code, waiting for results. Pure SFT is cheap but brittle: Imitation learning from teacher trajectories works, but degrades on out-of-distribution inputs. PivotRL (Yi et al., 2026) is a middle ground: 1 Start with offline expert trajectories (from teacher models) 2 Find “pivot turns” – turns where the model is uncertain about what to do next 3 Apply RL only at those turns, using a reward that credits functionally similar actions Think of it as: “Don’t re-learn what you already know. Focus your RL budget on the decisions that actually matter.” Result: Much cheaper than end-to-end RL, without the distribution-shift problems of pure SFT. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 28 / 39 SWE-RL: The Hardest Environment Task: Given a real GitHub issue, autonomously produce a code patch that passes all tests. Each RL rollout: 1 Launch a container with the real codebase 2 The model interacts with a terminal: reads code, explores the repo, writes a patch 3 Run the ground-truth test suite on the patch 4 Reward: 1 if all tests pass, 0 otherwise Why it’s separate from RLVR: SWE rollouts take minutes (vs. seconds for math/code verification), use 10–50+ turns, and need up to 64K tokens. Mixing them with fast environments creates a throughput bottleneck. Multi-harness training: The model trains with multiple CLI tool formats (OpenCode, Codex, etc.) – so it generalizes across agent frameworks at deployment. CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 29 / 39 RLHF: The Final Polish After RLVR and SWE-RL, a final RLHF stage improves general interaction quality. Innovation: Principle-following GenRM. Instead of a scalar reward model, use a generative model (Qwen3-235B) that explains its judgment The GenRM is conditioned on explicit behavioral principles (e.g., “be helpful but refuse unsafe requests”) This allows fine-grained control over the model’s behavior on safety and identity topics Why not use RLHF for everything? RLHF rewards are noisy (neural network judges can be fooled) RLVR rewards are exact (programmatic verification) Use RLVR where you can verify; use RLHF where you can’t CS 115B – Spring 2026 (James Pustejovsky) MoE & Agentic Training April 14, 2026 30 / 39 Safety Training: Attack and Defend Two safety RL environments: Anti-over-refusal: The model is rewarded for answering benign queries that look sensitive. Otherwise it learns to refuse anything remotely edgy. Anti-jailbreak: An adversarial loop: 1 Attack an

text: Recitation: Quiz 2 Review Concepts and Papers from CNNs to Scaling Laws Timothy Obiso Department of Computer Science Brandeis University COSI 115b — Spring 2026 1 / 45 Today’s Plan 1. CNNs & RNNs 2. Attention 3. Transformers 4. Large Language Models 5. Post-training & RL 6. Scaling Laws 7. Mixture-of-Experts For each: the core idea, the key paper(s), and what they contributed. 2 / 45 CNNs for Text — Kim (2014) Before Transformers, convolutional networks were a strong, simple baseline for sentence-level tasks. Key paper: Kim, “Convolutional Neural Networks for Sentence Classification” (EMNLP 2014). Contribution: • A simple CNN on top of pretrained word embeddings gets competitive results on many classification benchmarks • Popularized multi-width filters + max-over-time pooling for text 3 / 45 How a Text CNN Works 1. Embed each word ⇒ matrix of shape n × d 2. Apply 1D convolutions of widths k ∈ {3, 4, 5} in parallel • Each filter of width k captures k-gram patterns • Many filters per width 3. Max-over-time pool each filter’s output ⇒ one scalar per filter 4. Concatenate ⇒ fixed-size vector, feed to a classifier Convolution output length: kernel size k, stride 1, no padding, input length n ⇒ output length n − k + 1. Why Max-Over-Time? Max-pooling collapses the filter’s output to one scalar regardless of sentence length. This is what makes CNNs work for variable-length input. 4 / 45 Recurrent Neural Networks At each timestep: ht = tanh(Wh ht−1 + Wx xt + b) A recurrent network processes a sequence one token at a time, passing a hidden state forward. Why RNNs instead of CNNs? • Naturally handle variable-length input • Model dependencies across arbitrary distances (in principle) But: vanilla RNNs suffer from the vanishing gradient problem. 5 / 45 Vanishing & Exploding Gradients Backpropagation through time multiplies gradients by Wh repeatedly: k Y ∂ht−i+1 ∂ht = ∂ht−k ∂ht−i i=1 • ∥Wh ∥ < 1: gradients shrink exponentially ⇒ vanishing • ∥Wh ∥ > 1: gradients grow exponentially ⇒ exploding Consequence Vanilla RNNs can’t learn long-range dependencies. Exploding gradients are usually fixable with clipping; vanishing gradients require a structural fix — which is what LSTMs and GRUs provide. 6 / 45 LSTMs Long Short-Term Memory (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) adds a separate cell state ct and three sigmoid gates: • Forget gate ft : how much of old cell state to keep • Input gate it : how much new candidate info to write • Output gate ot : how much cell state to expose as hidden Cell state update: ct = ft ⊙ ct−1 + it ⊙ gt Why It Works The update is additive, not multiplicative. Gradients flow through ct along a “constant error carousel” — the path that mitigates vanishing gradients. 7 / 45 GRUs — Cho et al. (2014) Key paper: Cho, van Merriënboer, Bahdanau, Bengio, “Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder–Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation.” Contribution: introduces • The GRU (gated recurrent unit) — simpler than LSTM • The encoder–decoder framework for neural MT GRU gates: • Reset gate rt : how much of past hidden state to ignore • Update gate zt : interpolates between old and new hidden state Fewer parameters than LSTM, no separate cell state, often comparable performance. 8 / 45 Encoder–Decoder for Machine Translation Encoder x1 x2 Decoder x3 context c y1 y2 y3 • Encoder reads source sentence, compresses it into a fixed-dim context vector (final hidden state) • Decoder conditions on the context and generates the target autoregressively The Bottleneck A single fixed-dim vector has to carry an entire sentence’s worth of information. This motivates attention. 9 / 45 The Attention Idea “Don’t squeeze the whole source into one vector. Let the decoder look back at every source position.” Instead of a single context vector, attention gives the decoder a soft, differentiable lookup over all encoder positions. Key paper: Vaswani et al., “Attention Is All You Need” (NeurIPS 2017). Contribution: showed that you can replace recurrence entirely with attention and get better results, faster training (parallelism), and longer-range modeling. 10 / 45 Queries, Keys, and Values Attention is a differentiable lookup with three roles: • Query Q — “what am I looking for?” • Key K — “what do I have?” • Value V — “what do I return if you match me?” Each input token produces a query, a key, and a value (via learned linear projections). Attention scores between positions are computed from queries and keys; the values are what get aggregated. 11 / 45 Scaled Dot-Product Attention QK ⊤ Attention(Q, K , V ) = softmax √ dk   V Steps: 1. Compute similarity: QK ⊤ (dot product between each query and each key) √ 2. Scale by dk 3. Softmax over keys ⇒ attention weights that sum to 1 4. Weighted sum of values Why Scale by √ dk ? Without scaling, large dk produces large-magnitude dot products, pushing softmax into saturation where gradients vanish. Scaling keeps softmax in a useful regime regardless of head dimension. 12 / 45 Multi-Head Attention Instead of one attention with dk = dmodel , run h attentions in parallel with dk = dmodel /h, concatenate outputs. Why? • Different heads attend to different linguistic relationships — e.g., syntactic dependency, coreference, positional proximity • Same total compute as one big head, richer representation • A single head averages everything into one attention distribution and loses the diversity For dmodel = 512 and h = 8 heads: dk = 64 per head. 13 / 45 Self-Attention vs. Cross-Attention Self-attention Q, K , V all from the same sequence. A position attends to other positions in its own sequence. Cross-attention Q from one sequence (e.g., decoder), K , V from another (e.g., encoder). Used in encoder–decoder architectures. Masking variants of self-attention: • Bidirectional: each position sees all positions (BERT) • Causal / masked: position i sees only positions ≤ i (GPT) 14 / 45 The Transformer — Vaswani et al. (2017) The original Transformer is an encoder–decoder architecture for machine translation. Each block is just two sublayers: 1. Multi-head self-attention (+ residual + LayerNorm) 2. Feed-forward network (+ residual + LayerNorm) Why it worked so well: • Fully parallel over positions (unlike RNNs) ⇒ much faster training • Constant path length between any two positions ⇒ long-range dependencies • Scales gracefully with more layers, heads, data, compute 15 / 45 Positional Encodings Self-attention is permutation-equivariant. It doesn’t know token order. Solution: add position information to the token embedding before feeding to the network. Variants: • Sinusoidal (Vaswani et al., 2017): fixed, deterministic function of position  PE(pos,2i) = sin pos  100002i/d • Learned (BERT, GPT-2): position embedding table, trained jointly • Rotary / ALiBi (modern): inject position into the attention computation The original Transformer used sinusoidal; BERT switched to learned. 16 / 45 Residual Connections and LayerNorm Residual connections: output = x + sublayer(x) • Direct gradient path through many layers • Sublayer can learn a near-identity mapping if not useful ⇒ adding layers can’t hurt • Makes very deep stacks trainable Layer normalization: • Normalizes activations per-position across feature dim • Stabilizes training dynamics • Essentially every modern Transformer uses some variant (pre-norm, post-norm, RMSNorm, etc) 17 / 45 BERT — Devlin et al. (2019) Key paper: “BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding” (NAACL 2019). Architecture: encoder-only, bidirectional self-attention. Pretraining objective: masked language modeling (MLM) • Mask ˜15% of input tokens • Model predicts them using full bidirectional context • Loss computed only on masked positions What It Unlocked Strong general-purpose contextual representations. Fine-tune a small head on top for classification, NER, QA, NLI — and get state-of-the-art across the board. 18 / 45 GPT — Radford et al. (2018) Key paper: “Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training.” Architecture: decoder-only, causal (triangular) self-attention. Pretraining objective: causal language modeling (CLM) • Predict next token given past • Loss computed on every position • Autoregressive factorization: P(x1 , . . . , xn ) = Q t P(xt | x<t ) Later scaled up: GPT-2 (1.5B), GPT-3 (175B), etc. The line of work that established decoder-only as the dominant architecture for LLMs. 19 / 45 Three Transformer Families • Encoder-only (BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa) • Bidirectional attention • Best for classification, tagging, retrieval, embeddings • Cannot generate autoregressively • Decoder-only (GPT, Llama, Mistral) • Causal attention • Best for open-ended generation, dialogue, prompting • Can also do classification via prompting • Encoder–decoder (original Transformer, T5, BART) • Bidirectional encoder, causal decoder, cross-attention • Best for sequence-to-sequence (translation, summarization) 20 / 45 Scaling Up Language Models From 2018 onward: bigger models, more data, more compute. Surprising capabilities emerged along the way. Key question: what does a large language model trained only on next-token prediction actually know how to do? Two papers on the reading list answer different pieces of that: • Brown et al. (2020) — GPT-3 and in-context learning • Wei et al. (2022) — chain-of-thought prompting 21 / 45 In-Context Learning — Brown et al. (2020) Key paper: “Language Models are Few-Shot Learners” (NeurIPS 2020). The surprise: you can get GPT-3 to do a new task just by showing it examples in the prompt. No weight updates. No fine-tuning. Three evaluation regimes: • Zero-shot: task description only, no examples • One-shot: task description + one example, then target • Few-shot: task description + several examples, then target Key Point In-context learning is inference-only. Weights are frozen. Learning happens purely through conditioning on the prompt. 22 / 45 In-Context Learning Grows With Scale Central finding: the gap between few-shot and zero-shot performance grows with model size. • Small models: few-shot barely helps • Large models (175B): few-shot gives substantial gains on many tasks Interpretation In-context learning is itself an emergent capability of scale — not a property of any language model. What this changed: the focus of the field shifted from task-specific fine-tuning to prompt engineering and general-purpose models. 23 / 45 Chain-of-Thought — Wei et al. (2022) Key paper: “Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models” (NeurIPS 2022). Idea: prompt the model to produce intermediate reasoning steps before the final answer. Two common forms: • Few-shot CoT: examples in the prompt include step-by-step work • Zero-shot CoT: append “Let’s think step by step.” Large gains on multi-step reasoning: arithmetic word problems, commonsense, logic. 24 / 45 CoT is an Emergent Ability Below a certain model scale, CoT prompting doesn’t help — and can hurt. Why? • Small models produce incoherent reasoning chains • Noise in the scratchpad distracts from the final answer At large scale (∼60B+ in the paper): • Chains become coherent • Model effectively has more serial compute to solve multi-step problems Pattern to Recognize This is part of a broader pattern of emergent abilities: capabilities that appear suddenly at scale and can’t be extrapolated from smaller models. 25 / 45 Why Post-Training? A pretrained LM can predict the next token — but that’s not the same as being useful. Base model problems: • Continues prompts rather than answering them • No preference for being helpful, harmless, honest • Will happily hallucinate, refuse wrong things, or repeat itself Post-training Goal Align the pretrained model with human preferences, without retraining from scratch. 26 / 45 InstructGPT — Ouyang et al. (2022) Key paper: “Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback.” Three-stage training pipeline: 1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): fine-tune the pretrained LM on human-written demonstrations of desired behavior 2. Reward modeling: train a separate model to score outputs, from pairwise human preference judgments 3. RL with PPO: optimize the LM against the reward model Headline Result The 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT was preferred by human evaluators over the 175B-parameter base GPT-3. Alignment can matter more than raw scale. 27 / 45 The RLHF Pipeline Pretraining SFT large corpus human demos Reward model PPO RL with RM init init policy Detail Worth Knowing The reward model and the RL-tuned policy are both initialized from the SFT model, not trained from scratch. 28 / 45 Why a Separate Reward Model? Why not ask humans to rate outputs directly during RL? • Cost: RL requires scoring millions of generations. Human labeling at that scale is impossible. • Consistency: humans are better at comparing two outputs than at rating them on a scale. Pairwise preferences are less noisy. • Generalization: the RM must score novel outputs generated during training. A learned model generalizes from the fixed preference dataset. • Speed: RL needs a reward signal at every gradient step. Humans can’t keep up. 29 / 45 PPO — Schulman et al. (2017) Key paper: “Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms.” A policy-gradient method that’s both stable and sample-efficient. The trick — clipping: h i LCLIP (θ) = E min rt Ât , clip(rt , 1 − ϵ, 1 + ϵ)Ât where rt (θ) = πθ (a|s)/πold (a|s) is the policy ratio. What Clipping Buys Us The policy can’t move too far in a single update. Trust-region-like stability without the complexity of TRPO. RLHF also adds a KL penalty against the SFT model to prevent drift and reward hacking. 30 / 45 Kaplan et al. (2020) Key paper: “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models.” Finding: test loss follows a power-law in three quantities: L(N) ∝ N −α , L(D) ∝ D −β , L(C ) ∝ C −γ where N = parameters, D = tokens, C = compute. What “power-law” actually means: • Each doubling of N gives a constant relative (multiplicative) reduction in loss • Not a constant absolute reduction — absolute gains shrink as loss shrinks • Loss vs. N on log-log axes ⇒ a straight line 31 / 45 Scaling Laws in Practice Why do labs run scaling-law experiments? • Run many small models cheaply • Fit a power-law • Extrapolate to predict the loss of a single very large run • Pick the best (N, D) pair for your compute budget Compute budget approximation: C ≈ 6ND. Given a fixed C , this tells you how to trade off model size and tokens. The Takeaway Scaling laws aren’t just theory — they’re the primary planning tool at frontier labs. 32 / 45 Chinchilla — Hoffmann et al. (2022) Key paper: “Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models.” Finding: the Kaplan recipe was wrong about allocation. • Kaplan (2020): scale N fast, let D lag • Chinchilla (2022): N and D should grow together — roughly D ≈ 20N The Experiment Chinchilla (70B parameters, 1.4T tokens) vs. Gopher (280B parameters, 300B tokens) — same compute budget. Chinchilla outperformed Gopher across the board. Previous models were undertrained. 33 / 45 Modern Practice Today’s LLMs are typically trained on far more tokens than Chinchilla-optimal. Example: Llama 3 (8B parameters) trained on roughly 15 trillion tokens — well past the D ≈ 20N ratio. Why? • Inference cost scales with N, not D • A smaller, “over-trained” model is cheaper per query • For models that will serve many queries, the trade is worth it: you spend more training compute once, save serving compute forever Chinchilla-optimality is about training efficiency. Real deployment often trades that for inference efficiency. 34 / 45 Why Mixture-of-Experts? Scaling laws say: more parameters ⇒ lower loss. But more parameters also means more compute per token. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) breaks that link: • Replace a single large feed-forward layer with E smaller “expert” FFNs • For each token, a router picks only k experts (typically k = 1 or 2) • Only the chosen experts’ weights are used for that token The Payoff Total parameters grow with E (more capacity, lower loss). Compute per token grows only with k (typically constant). You get a huge model at a small model’s inference cost. 35 / 45 The Foundational Paper — Shazeer et al. (2017) Key paper: Shazeer, Mirhoseini, Maziarz, Davis, Le, Hinton, Dean, “Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer” (ICLR 2017). Contribution: • Sparsely-gated MoE layer: top-k routing with a learned gating network • Showed MoE scales to hundreds of billions of parameters with per-token compute barely increased • Introduced the load-balancing loss used by nearly every MoE since Pre-dates Transformers — applied to LSTM language models originally — but the recipe carried over directly. 36 / 45 Anatomy of an MoE Layer top-k token x Router E1 E2 output y ··· EE Per token: 1. Router computes a score for each of the E experts 2. Pick the top-k experts (typically k = 1 or 2) 3. Run the token through just those experts 4. Output is a gated weighted sum of their outputs 37 / 45 The Router The router is typically a single linear layer plus softmax: g (x) = softmax(Wr x) Top-k routing keeps the largest k entries and zeroes the rest: X y= gi (x) · Ei (x) i∈top-k(g (x)) Design choices that matter: • k = 1 (Switch Transformer): cheapest, hardest to train stably • k = 2 (original Shazeer, Mixtral): more robust, slightly more compute • Noise during training: adds exploration so the router doesn’t collapse onto a single expert 38 / 45 The Load-Balancing Problem Without constraints, the router tends to collapse: it sends nearly all tokens to a small subset of experts. Why that’s bad: • Most experts get no gradient signal ⇒ they’re dead weight • The model’s effective capacity is much smaller than E experts • Parallelism across devices (each expert on a different GPU) becomes useless — one GPU does all the work The Fix: Load-Balancing Loss Add an auxiliary loss that penalizes uneven expert usage over a batch. Encourages each expert to see roughly 1/E of the tokens. This is not a constraint at inference — just during training. 39 / 45 Switch Transformer — Fedus et al. (2022) Key paper: Fedus, Zoph, Shazeer, “Switch Transformer: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity” (JMLR 2022). Contribution: • Showed k = 1 routing (“hard switch”) works well and is cheaper than k = 2 • Scaled MoE Transformers to 1.6 trillion parameters • Careful engineering: capacity factors, routing precision in fp32, expert parallelism Why It Mattered Demonstrated that MoE isn’t just a clever trick — it’s a practical recipe for reaching parameter counts that are infeasible with dense models, while keeping inference cost manageable. 40 / 45 Modern MoE: Mixtral and DeepSeek Post-2023, MoE became standard in frontier open models. Mixtral 8x7B (Mistral AI, 2024): • 8 experts per layer, k = 2 • Total parameters: ∼47B. Active per token: ∼13B. • Matches or beats Llama 2 70B on most benchmarks at a fraction of the inference cost DeepSeek-V3 / DeepSeek MoE (2024–2025): • Hundreds of experts, fine-grained routing • Shared experts (always active) + routed experts (top-k) • 671B total, ∼37B active per token 41 / 45 MoE vs. Dense: The Trade-off Params per token Total params Training FLOPs Memory (inference) Parallelism style Dense MoE all of them = per-token params proportional to params proportional to params tensor / pipeline only top-k experts ≫ per-token params proportional to active params proportional to total params expert parallelism total total Key Point MoE reduces compute, not memory. You still have to fit all the experts somewhere — it doesn’t give you a free lunch on GPU RAM. 42 / 45 Open Problems in MoE MoE is powerful but far from solved. • Router stability: top-k is discrete ⇒ routing decisions have no gradient. Training is sensitive to initialization, capacity factors, and load-balance weight. • Fine-tuning is fragile: MoEs can forget or collapse routing patterns during fine-tuning and
